profiles.name: 5-Amino-1MQ
profiles.summary: 5-Amino-1MQ is a small-molecule inhibitor of nicotinamide N-methyltransferase, not a peptide. Mouse and cell studies report metabolic effects, but they do not establish effective human weight loss, improved longevity or a validated safety profile for commercial products.
profiles.description: Also written 5A1MQ or 5-amino-1-methylquinolinium, this compound is included because it appears in peptide-oriented catalogs despite its different chemistry. The experimental target, NNMT, participates in nicotinamide methylation and links to cellular energy and methyl-donor metabolism. Original studies used cultured adipocytes and diet-induced obese mice, with later work examining liver and metabolic outcomes. These findings support target investigation. They do not establish that blocking NNMT is beneficial in every tissue or that self-administered oral or injectable preparations reproduce the exposure achieved in controlled animal experiments.
profiles.mechanism: NNMT converts nicotinamide to 1-methylnicotinamide using S-adenosylmethionine as a methyl donor. Inhibiting it can change intracellular nicotinamide-related metabolites, NAD-associated pathways and methyl-donor availability. Experimental 5-amino-1MQ studies connect those changes to reduced lipogenesis and altered energy handling. NNMT has tissue-specific functions, so a proposed metabolic benefit cannot be reduced to the claim that raising NAD is automatically beneficial throughout the body.
profiles.keyTakeaway: 5-Amino-1MQ is a preclinical small molecule, not an established peptide therapy. Its animal findings and target biology warrant research but do not provide human efficacy, interaction or long-term safety evidence.

sections.title: Early metabolic experiments
sections.body: The original inhibitor study found reduced lipogenesis in cultured adipocytes and lower body weight and adipose mass in obese mice. The authors linked effects to changes in metabolic regulators, but did not establish a human weight-management treatment.

sections.title: Later obesity and liver findings
sections.body: A 2024 mouse study reported improvements in glucose tolerance, insulin sensitivity and liver fat-related pathology, alongside pharmacokinetic and tissue-distribution work. These are preclinical outcomes and should not be described as demonstrated reversal of human MASH.

sections.title: Why a target is not a treatment
sections.body: A compound can inhibit the intended enzyme yet have inadequate exposure, off-target activity or an unfavorable safety margin in people. Dose-response and tissue-distribution data from mice do not supply a clinically validated human regimen.

sections.title: Human uncertainty
sections.body: The cited research does not establish adverse-event frequencies, reproductive safety, long-term toxicity or drug interactions in humans. Short animal studies with no obvious toxicity cannot answer those questions. Product identity and purity add separate uncertainties outside regulated development.

sections.title: Why it is labeled nonpeptide
sections.body: Its methylquinolinium scaffold is not an amino-acid chain. Keeping that distinction visible prevents readers from assuming it shares the pharmacology, manufacturing requirements or clinical evidence of approved peptide medicines merely because sellers group them together.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.body:
Is 5-Amino-1MQ actually a peptide? No. It is a small-molecule NNMT inhibitor and is included here because it appears in the reference catalog.

Have its animal weight and liver findings been established in patients? The cited studies are preclinical. They do not establish a human clinical benefit, a safe treatment regimen or a replacement for approved obesity or liver-disease care.

profiles.name: Abaloparatide
profiles.summary: Abaloparatide is a bone-forming prescription medicine for adults with osteoporosis at high fracture risk. It activates the parathyroid hormone type 1 receptor. Its strongest fracture-prevention evidence is in postmenopausal women; the indication in men is supported by increased bone mineral density.
profiles.description: Abaloparatide belongs to the anabolic osteoporosis medicines: treatment stimulates production of new bone rather than principally slowing bone breakdown. The US product Tymlos is a subcutaneous injection used for postmenopausal osteoporosis at high fracture risk and to increase bone density in men at high risk. Previous fragility fractures, multiple risk factors, or failure or intolerance of other osteoporosis treatments help define the labeled population. It is structurally related to parathyroid hormone-related protein, not a growth hormone secretagogue. A favorable effect on bone density is clinically relevant, but the amount and type of fracture-outcome evidence differ between the populations studied.
profiles.mechanism: Abaloparatide binds PTH1 receptors on bone-forming cells and activates cyclic AMP signaling. Intermittent receptor stimulation increases osteoblast activity and bone formation, with associated changes in bone remodeling. This pharmacology differs from chronically excessive endogenous parathyroid hormone, which can drive net bone loss. Its relationship to PTH-related protein explains the shared receptor with teriparatide, while the two medicines remain different molecules with separate trial programs and product instructions.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Abaloparatide has established osteoporosis indications and fracture data in postmenopausal women. Its clinical value depends on fracture risk, treatment sequencing, and calcium-related safety; it is not an established therapy for ordinary exercise recovery or generalized rejuvenation.

atAGlance.label: Evidence distinction
atAGlance.value: Fracture reduction in women; bone-density indication in men

sections.title: Who is it used for?
sections.body: The approved uses concern osteoporosis at high fracture risk. In postmenopausal women, the label includes reduction of vertebral and nonvertebral fractures. In men, the indication is to increase bone density. These are distinct claims: a study showing improved bone density should not automatically be described as having proved fewer hip fractures in every treated group.

sections.title: Clinical evidence
sections.body: The ACTIVE trial compared abaloparatide with placebo and included an open-label teriparatide group in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. Abaloparatide reduced new vertebral fractures and improved bone density. The study supports its osteoporosis role, but was not designed to establish benefits for athletic recovery, normal aging, or people with healthy bone strength.

sections.title: Calcium and bone-tumor precautions
sections.body: Important risks include hypersensitivity, dizziness or postural hypotension, increased blood calcium, increased urinary calcium, and possible worsening of kidney-stone risk. Osteosarcoma occurred in rats; the label advises avoiding people with elevated baseline osteosarcoma risk. Human observational evidence has not demonstrated an increased osteosarcoma rate, but information about prolonged exposure remains limited.

sections.title: How does it fit into osteoporosis care?
sections.body: A bone-forming treatment is one part of a longer fracture-prevention plan. Follow-up considers bone density, fractures, mineral metabolism, and subsequent therapy to preserve gains. The current label limits routine cumulative use because long-duration evidence is limited. Tymlos approval does not establish the quality, equivalence, or safety of a research-vendor abaloparatide product.

sections.title: Is abaloparatide interchangeable with teriparatide?
sections.body: Both activate PTH1 receptors and can stimulate bone formation, but they are different medicines with separate labels and evidence. A shared mechanism does not establish identical effects or eligibility. Abaloparatide’s fracture evidence and male bone-density indication should be interpreted within the populations actually studied.

profiles.name: Acetyl hexapeptide-8
profiles.summary: Acetyl hexapeptide-8 is a topical cosmetic peptide commonly associated with Argireline. Small controlled studies suggest an effect on wrinkle appearance, but they do not establish equivalence to injected botulinum toxin. Delivery through intact skin and the finished formulation remain important limitations.
profiles.description: This six-amino-acid ingredient was previously described as acetyl hexapeptide-3; the older name appears in research and should be searchable as an alias. It is chemically different from acetyl octapeptide-3, despite the easily confused numbers. The cosmetic rationale concerns expression-related lines, but evaluating that claim requires more than a laboratory mechanism. A topical product must preserve the peptide and deliver it to a relevant site, while its moisturizer base can independently change the appearance of fine lines. Human evidence is therefore best interpreted at the level of the tested formulation, duration, and measurement method.
profiles.mechanism: The peptide was designed from a region of SNAP-25, a protein involved in the SNARE machinery used for vesicle release. Experimental work proposes interference with transmitter-release processes. That is a different molecule and mode of delivery from botulinum toxin. Demonstrating a proposed interaction in a laboratory does not show that a cosmetic cream reaches human neuromuscular targets with an equivalent magnitude or duration of effect.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Acetyl hexapeptide-8 has some direct cosmetic trial evidence, but the realistic claim concerns modest formulation-specific changes in wrinkle appearance. It should not be presented as a proven topical replacement for injectable botulinum toxin.

sections.title: The randomized human study
sections.body: A four-week trial randomized sixty Chinese participants to an Argireline formulation or placebo in a three-to-one ratio. Subjective grading and silicone-replica analysis favored the active preparation. The small sample and short follow-up limit conclusions about persistence, uncommon adverse effects, and performance of other products containing the same ingredient.

sections.title: Why the older name matters
sections.body: A separate small study used the name acetyl hexapeptide-3 and examined it alone or with tripeptide-10 citrulline. That is evidence concerning acetyl hexapeptide-8’s historical naming, not evidence for acetyl octapeptide-3. Confusing the names would assign a clinical study to the wrong molecule.

sections.title: Cosmetic evidence has a defined scope
sections.body: The CIR document reviews this ingredient in cosmetic use and clarifies its naming; its conclusions cannot be extended to injection or arbitrary formulations. Cosmetic status is not FDA drug approval. The finished product’s tolerability, vehicle, and stability remain relevant to interpreting any reported benefit.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions
sections.body:
Is acetyl hexapeptide-3 the same as acetyl hexapeptide-8?
It is an older name for the ingredient described here. Acetyl octapeptide-3 is a different molecule.

Is Argireline proven equivalent to Botox?
No. Small topical cosmetic studies measured wrinkle appearance, not clinical equivalence to injected botulinum toxin. Molecule, delivery, exposure, magnitude of effect, and duration all differ.

profiles.name: Acetyl octapeptide-3
profiles.summary: Acetyl octapeptide-3, commonly associated with SNAP-8, is a cosmetic ingredient marketed for expression-line appearance. Direct evidence for the isolated ingredient is limited. Studies of multi-ingredient microneedle patches cannot establish the effect of ordinary topical SNAP-8 products on their own.
profiles.description: The eight-residue ingredient acetyl octapeptide-3 should not be confused with acetyl hexapeptide-3, an older name for acetyl hexapeptide-8. That naming distinction changes which studies are relevant. SNAP-8 is a commercial ingredient context, not a synonym for botulinum toxin or proof of a clinically equivalent effect. Published work includes formulations that combine the peptide with other actives and a delivery device. Such a product may change skin appearance, yet the result cannot identify which component produced the change. The vehicle, hydration, physical microneedling effect, and other ingredients are all plausible contributors requiring controlled comparison.
profiles.mechanism: The ingredient is marketed around modulation of expression-related signaling, building on the SNAP-25-inspired cosmetic-peptide concept. A proposed neurotransmission mechanism does not demonstrate that a conventional cream reaches the relevant neural structures. Microneedle delivery intentionally changes the skin barrier, so evidence from that delivery system cannot be treated as evidence that simple application to intact skin has the same exposure or effect.
profiles.keyTakeaway: For SNAP-8, ingredient identity and delivery method are decisive. A combined microneedle study cannot isolate the peptide’s effect, and acetyl hexapeptide-3 studies investigate a chemically different ingredient.

sections.title: What the patch study can establish
sections.body: A 12-week single-center study evaluated hyaluronic-acid microneedle patches containing acetyl octapeptide-3, other peptides, adenosine, and seaweed extracts. Instrumental measurements improved and the product was tolerated in that study. Because it tested a combined product and delivery system, the findings do not quantify the independent effect of acetyl octapeptide-3.

sections.title: A common citation mismatch
sections.body: The trial titled as a combination of tripeptide-10 citrulline and acetyl hexapeptide-3 does not study acetyl octapeptide-3. The molecule name differs even though both appear in expression-line marketing. That study therefore cannot establish SNAP-8 efficacy, even when a product description cites it alongside claims about expression lines.

sections.title: Cosmetic scope
sections.body: The manufacturer identifies SNAP-8 as a cosmetic ingredient solution. That identity does not establish an injectable use or unrestricted safety of raw material. Cosmetic status is not FDA drug approval. Product-specific tolerability and appropriate evidence for the delivery method remain necessary.

profiles.name: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5
profiles.summary: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is a cosmetic ingredient associated with the original Eyeseryl eye-contour products. Independent evidence isolating its contribution to puffiness or dark circles is sparse. A study of an injected multi-component product cannot validate a topical cream or the peptide alone.
profiles.description: The ingredient’s identity is more specific than the general category eye peptide: acetyl tetrapeptide-5 has a defined four-residue structure and is associated with the Eyeseryl name. Eye-contour appearance can reflect pigment, fluid, skin texture, and underlying anatomy, so a single cosmetic claim can hide several different endpoints. Supplier descriptions and product availability establish commercial use, not a clinically proven treatment for eyelid swelling. Newer products carrying expanded versions of a trade name may also contain different peptides. The actual ingredient list matters more than assuming every similarly named eye-care product is chemically identical.
profiles.mechanism: The cosmetic concept concerns the appearance of puffiness and the surrounding skin, but an independently established clinical mechanism for the isolated ingredient was not demonstrated in the sources checked. Claims about fluid movement, vascular permeability, or collagen protection need direct testing. Changes after a formulation containing hyaluronic acid, amino acids, and this peptide cannot identify which pathway, if any, was specifically influenced by acetyl tetrapeptide-5.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is a defined cosmetic ingredient with limited isolated clinical evidence. Keep the original Eyeseryl identity, finished-product claims, and injection-combination studies separate; they answer different questions about benefit and safety.

atAGlance.label: Route boundary
atAGlance.value: Topical cosmetics and injections are separate

sections.title: A recent combination study does not isolate the peptide
sections.body: A 2026 single-arm study of forty women assessed an injected hyaluronic-acid and amino-acid product that also contained an Eyeseryl complex. Ultrasound and elasticity measurements changed after treatment. There was no untreated or placebo comparison, and the authors acknowledged confounding. The study cannot establish that acetyl tetrapeptide-5 caused the changes or that a topical product would reproduce them.

sections.title: What supplier records establish
sections.body: Lubrizol identifies an Eyeseryl peptide solution product, while a research-material safety sheet specifies acetyl tetrapeptide-5’s chemical identity. Those records support naming and material characterization. They are not controlled evidence that a consumer cream reduces all causes of under-eye swelling or that research powder is suitable for human treatment.

sections.title: Limits of the cosmetic category
sections.body: Cosmetic status is not FDA drug approval. The safety of a complete eye-area product depends on more than the peptide name, and tolerability of one formulation cannot establish safety on damaged skin or by injection. Appearance claims should remain distinct from treatment claims for an underlying eye or systemic condition.

profiles.name: Afamelanotide
profiles.summary: Afamelanotide is the active ingredient in a prescription implant used for adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria. Melanotan I is a historical name for the molecule. The approved medical use is distinct from unapproved products marketed for cosmetic tanning.
profiles.description: Erythropoietic protoporphyria, or EPP, can cause severe pain after light exposure and markedly restrict daily life. Afamelanotide was developed to increase the amount of light exposure patients can tolerate without pain. Its approved implant is administered within a specialist care framework. Afamelanotide and Melanotan I identify the same molecule, while the approved implant and unapproved tanning products have very different clinical and regulatory contexts. Approval of Scenesse does not mean that every vial or spray carrying a related name has the same composition, delivery, evidence, or quality. Melanotan II is a different molecule with its own evidence and safety concerns.
profiles.mechanism: Afamelanotide activates melanocortin-1 receptors and increases eumelanin production. The pigment response can improve light tolerance in EPP, where abnormal protoporphyrin accumulation makes light exposure painful. This mechanism does not correct the underlying enzyme defect and does not establish general protection against skin cancer. The relevant clinical endpoint is pain-free light exposure, not simply a darker skin color.
profiles.keyTakeaway: One molecule can have an approved specialist product and unapproved commercial lookalikes. Afamelanotide’s evidence concerns EPP and pain-free light exposure; it should not be translated into a blanket endorsement of cosmetic tanning products.

sections.title: What the randomized studies measured
sections.body: Two placebo-controlled trials in Europe and the United States enrolled 74 and 94 patients, respectively. Afamelanotide increased pain-free time in direct sunlight and improved quality-of-life measures. The trial endpoints were tied to a rare, debilitating photosensitivity disorder. They do not establish benefit for people seeking a cosmetic tan or permission to abandon sun protection.

sections.title: Pigment changes require follow-up
sections.body: The label describes darkening of existing nevi and other pigmentation changes, with regular full-body skin examinations recommended. Implant-site reactions and nausea are additional considerations. A pigment-producing mechanism is therefore accompanied by a surveillance requirement, rather than being assumed harmless because it resembles a naturally occurring hormone pathway.

sections.title: Keep the product context visible
sections.body: FDA approval covers the Scenesse implant for its specific adult EPP indication. An online Melanotan I product is not automatically that approved medicine. The historical alias does not change the importance of the exact formulation, administration route, quality controls, and authorized medical use.

profiles.name: Albiglutide
profiles.molecularClass: GLP-1 analog fused to human albumin
profiles.summary: Albiglutide is a long-acting GLP-1 medicine previously marketed for type 2 diabetes. It has randomized cardiovascular-outcome evidence, but its historical approvals must be distinguished from current availability: the European authorization was withdrawn after commercial discontinuation.
profiles.description: Albiglutide was marketed as Tanzeum in the United States and Eperzan in Europe. Its albumin-fusion design prolonged GLP-1 activity and supported weekly injection for adult type 2 diabetes. The HARMONY Outcomes study later demonstrated cardiovascular benefit in a high-risk diabetes population. Despite that clinical record, the manufacturer discontinued marketing, and the European Commission withdrew the Eperzan authorization in 2018 at the company’s request for commercial reasons. This profile preserves the evidence and approval history without implying that a currently obtainable albiglutide product is a routine treatment option in every market.
profiles.mechanism: The molecule joins modified GLP-1 sequences to human albumin, extending circulation time and protecting activity compared with native GLP-1. Receptor activation increases glucose-dependent insulin release, reduces inappropriate glucagon secretion and affects gastric emptying. Albumin fusion changes exposure and delivery but does not remove the physiological consequences of GLP-1 signaling, including gastrointestinal adverse effects and interactions with other glucose-lowering treatment.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Albiglutide is clinically important as an established GLP-1 research and treatment history, but a historical approval is not evidence of current supply. Its withdrawal and cardiovascular trial findings should both remain visible.

sections.title: Original approved indication
sections.body: The original FDA label approved albiglutide with diet and exercise for glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes. It was not an approved type 1 diabetes or obesity medicine.

sections.title: Cardiovascular findings
sections.body: HARMONY Outcomes enrolled patients with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease and found fewer major cardiovascular events with albiglutide than placebo. This later trial is more informative about cardiovascular efficacy than the older initial label’s statement that outcomes evidence was not yet available.

sections.title: Known adverse effects
sections.body: The historical label identifies gastrointestinal symptoms and injection-site reactions, with warnings about pancreatitis, serious allergy and hypoglycemia when combined with insulin or insulin secretagogues. Medullary thyroid carcinoma history and MEN2 were contraindications.

sections.title: Why the withdrawal matters
sections.body: EMA states that the European Commission withdrew Eperzan’s authorization on 29 October 2018 after the manufacturer permanently discontinued marketing for commercial reasons. That is different from claiming a demonstrated new safety failure caused the withdrawal.

sections.title: How this record should be used
sections.body: The article supports understanding of the GLP-1 class and historical evidence. It does not establish that an online albiglutide listing is an authorized or available replacement for a currently marketed diabetes medicine.

profiles.name: Amycretin
profiles.molecularClass: Unimolecular GLP-1 and amylin receptor agonist peptide
profiles.summary: Amycretin, now also known as zenagamtide, is an investigational peptide combining GLP-1 and amylin-related receptor activity in one molecule. Oral and injectable programs have shown metabolic effects in human trials, but their formulations, endpoints and evidence maturity differ.
profiles.description: Amycretin was the development name used in early studies of this single-molecule approach; 2026 research uses the name zenagamtide. The compound is distinct from CagriSema, which combines two separate active peptides. Both oral and subcutaneous formulations have entered clinical studies. Early obesity studies emphasized safety, exposure and exploratory weight change, while a 2026 oral phase 2 trial assessed glycated hemoglobin in type 2 diabetes. These different designs should not be collapsed into one promised weight-loss percentage or an assertion of established cardiovascular protection.
profiles.mechanism: The molecule activates GLP-1 and amylin-related signaling, with calcitonin receptor activity also described in the phase 2 publication. The goal is to combine glucose-regulating and satiety effects within one peptide rather than administering separate drugs. Delivery changes exposure: an oral peptide formulation must overcome gastrointestinal degradation and absorption barriers, so injectable and oral study results cannot be translated by comparing nominal amounts.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Amycretin/zenagamtide is a substantive clinical-development program, not an approved treatment at this review date. Its oral and injectable evidence should be read separately, with attention to study size and endpoints.

atAGlance.label: Design
atAGlance.value: Single peptide with multiple receptor activities

sections.title: What the trials investigate
sections.body: Development targets weight management and glucose control. The oral type 2 diabetes trial studied adults already receiving metformin with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor, so its results do not establish use in untreated diabetes or type 1 diabetes.

sections.title: Oral diabetes evidence
sections.body: In the 2026 phase 2 trial, 186 participants were randomized and followed for thirty-six weeks. Oral zenagamtide lowered HbA1c more than placebo across tested groups. The primary question was glycemic efficacy, not cardiovascular events or long-term obesity complications.

sections.title: Injectable obesity evidence
sections.body: The phase 1b/2a study included 125 participants across several cohorts and reported substantial exploratory weight reduction. A high number withdrew, including many for reasons unrelated to adverse events. Small cohorts and missing-data assumptions limit certainty around headline percentages.

sections.title: Tolerability and evidence gaps
sections.body: Gastrointestinal events predominated in oral and injectable studies. Early trials cannot reliably exclude uncommon or delayed harms. Pregnancy, pediatric use, combination with other appetite medicines and long-term outcomes require dedicated evidence rather than extrapolation from receptor targets.

sections.title: Is this the same as CagriSema?
sections.body: No. Amycretin/zenagamtide is one engineered molecule, while CagriSema uses cagrilintide plus semaglutide. Similar therapeutic concepts do not mean identical pharmacology, exposure, safety or regulatory status.

profiles.name: Angiotensin II
profiles.summary: Angiotensin II is a natural blood-pressure-regulating hormone and an approved intravenous vasopressor for adults with septic or other distributive shock. It can raise pressure when conventional vasopressors are insufficient. The pivotal evidence primarily concerns blood-pressure response, while thrombosis is an important safety concern.
profiles.description: Angiotensin II is part of the renin–angiotensin system that normally helps regulate circulation and sodium balance. The pharmaceutical product Giapreza supplies the active octapeptide directly during severe vasodilatory shock. This intensive-care use differs from chronic hypertension, where medicines often block the same pathway. In shock, clinicians may need an additional mechanism to restore vascular tone despite fluids and other vasopressors. The ATHOS-3 trial demonstrated a rapid pressure response in a selected critically ill population. Improving a hemodynamic measurement is clinically useful, but it should not be described automatically as proof of improved survival or prevention of organ failure in every patient.
profiles.mechanism: Angiotensin II binds angiotensin receptors, principally AT1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle, causing vasoconstriction and increased systemic vascular resistance. It also promotes aldosterone-related effects in normal physiology. Direct infusion bypasses upstream hormone generation. This mechanism complements catecholamine and vasopressin pathways, but stronger vascular tone can carry thrombotic or ischemic consequences, making circulation and organ perfusion important alongside the displayed blood-pressure value.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Angiotensin II is an established hospital vasopressor for defined shock states. Its strongest randomized evidence is for raising blood pressure; the benefit–risk assessment also includes thrombosis, perfusion, and the underlying cause of shock.

sections.title: A critical-care intervention
sections.body: Giapreza is indicated to increase blood pressure in adults with septic or other distributive shock. It is delivered as an intravenous infusion in a monitored setting. It does not treat the infectious source itself or replace fluid assessment, antimicrobial therapy when indicated, and management of the underlying shock process.

sections.title: The ATHOS-3 endpoint
sections.body: ATHOS-3 enrolled patients with vasodilatory shock requiring substantial background vasopressor support. More angiotensin II recipients met the prespecified early mean-arterial-pressure response than placebo recipients. That endpoint demonstrates vasopressor efficacy. The study did not establish a statistically definitive overall survival advantage, so claims about mortality should remain qualified.

sections.title: Thrombotic risk and competing goals
sections.body: The label warns about increased arterial and venous thrombotic events and calls for concurrent venous-thromboembolism prophylaxis unless contraindicated. Other vasopressors and shock itself also influence ischemic risk. Clinicians must assess tissue perfusion, organ function, and evolving hemodynamics rather than treating a pressure number in isolation.

sections.title: Why give a hormone often blocked in hypertension?
sections.body: The clinical context is different. Chronic excess vasoconstriction can contribute to hypertension, whereas profound loss of vascular tone in distributive shock can threaten organ perfusion. Replacing an active pressor signal in that emergency does not imply that angiotensin II is appropriate for chronic fatigue, general circulation support, or outpatient wellness.

profiles.name: AOD-9604
profiles.summary: AOD-9604 is a modified growth-hormone fragment investigated for obesity. Animal fat-metabolism findings did not translate into convincing human weight-loss efficacy, and a large clinical program was discontinued. It is not an FDA-approved obesity medicine or full-length growth-hormone replacement.
profiles.description: AOD-9604 consists of a tyrosine added to the 177–191 region of human growth hormone. That defined modified sequence matters because commercial descriptions often blur it with native Fragment 176–191. Early rodent work suggested effects on fat metabolism without the full growth-hormone receptor profile. Human obesity development subsequently failed to show adequate benefit over placebo in the large OPTIONS study. The molecule remains scientifically interesting, but that history should accompany claims about targeted fat loss rather than being replaced by selected positive animal results or unsupported claims of selective abdominal-fat reduction.
profiles.mechanism: Preclinical studies examined reduced lipogenesis, increased fat oxidation and lipolysis. One mouse and cell study found that AOD-9604 did not compete for the growth-hormone receptor or stimulate receptor-dependent proliferation in the tested system. This distinguishes it mechanistically from intact GH, but does not prove complete absence of endocrine or other effects in humans. A reliably validated human fat-loss mechanism has not emerged from the negative efficacy program.
profiles.keyTakeaway: AOD-9604 has a defined research identity and negative major obesity-trial history. It should not be presented as proven fat loss without GH-related risks, or automatically merged with every product labeled Fragment 176–191.

atAGlance.label: Human efficacy
atAGlance.value: Large trial did not beat placebo

sections.title: What animal studies found
sections.body: Studies in obese rats and mice reported altered fat metabolism and reduced weight gain. The tested species, exposure and outcome matter: reducing weight gain in an animal model is not the same as producing clinically useful weight loss in adults.

sections.title: The important negative trial
sections.body: FDA’s review describes the OPTIONS study, which enrolled 536 adults and found no significant weight-loss difference from placebo. The developer ended obesity development after that result. This is central evidence, not a minor omission from an otherwise proven treatment.

sections.title: Relationship to Fragment 176–191
sections.body: The analytical literature defines AOD-9604 as hGH 177–191 with an added N-terminal tyrosine. Native fragment nomenclature is not an assurance of that same sequence. Molecular identity must be established before evidence can be transferred between names.

sections.title: What safety claims cannot establish
sections.body: A lack of selected GH-like effects in preclinical experiments does not provide a complete human safety profile. Long-term use, injected preparations, immune responses and product purity require evidence specific to the formulation and route.

sections.title: Current clinical meaning
sections.body: AOD-9604 is not an FDA-approved drug for obesity. A compounding discussion, ingredient listing or food-related safety claim is not approval of an injectable weight-loss medicine and does not overturn the unsuccessful obesity efficacy evidence.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.body:
Did AOD-9604 demonstrate meaningful weight loss in its major obesity trial? FDA's review describes a large trial without statistically significant weight loss versus placebo. Animal metabolic findings do not overturn that result.

Is every vial called Fragment 176–191 chemically equivalent? No. AOD-9604 has a defined modified sequence; vendor shorthand alone cannot establish the identity or purity of another material.

profiles.name: Apraglutide
profiles.summary: Apraglutide is an investigational GLP-2 analog for short bowel syndrome with intestinal failure. A phase 3 trial showed reduced parenteral-support volume, but regulatory development continues, including an additional confirmatory study; it is not an approved substitute for teduglutide.
profiles.description: Apraglutide is designed to improve intestinal adaptation and absorption in people who need intravenous fluid or nutrition because too little functioning bowel remains. Its long action supports investigation as a weekly treatment. The STARS trial evaluated patients with different intestinal anatomies, including a stoma or colon in continuity. Not every secondary endpoint was positive, and treatment response cannot be inferred from the overall trial average alone. In 2025 the FDA requested another confirmatory phase 3 study, and the sponsor’s 2026 plans include STARS-2. This distinguishes demonstrated trial activity from a completed approval process.
profiles.mechanism: Apraglutide activates the GLP-2 receptor, supporting intestinal mucosal adaptation and absorptive function. Longer exposure is intended to reduce administration frequency relative to shorter-acting GLP-2 therapy. Increased uptake of fluid and nutrients may reduce parenteral-support requirements, but must be balanced against changing hydration needs. A trophic intestinal mechanism also creates questions about obstruction, abnormal tissue growth and long-term gastrointestinal surveillance that clinical development must resolve.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Apraglutide has phase 3 evidence for reducing parenteral support in intestinal failure, but confirmatory development remains necessary. Its clinical goal is measurable nutritional independence or reduced support, not nonspecific digestive enhancement.

sections.title: The population being studied
sections.body: The development program concerns short bowel syndrome with dependence on parenteral support. It does not test routine IBS or generalized gut-health claims, and anatomy-specific analyses help explain why responses may differ across patients.

sections.title: STARS primary result
sections.body: In 163 randomized and treated patients, weekly support volume fell by a mean 25.5% with apraglutide versus 12.5% with placebo at week twenty-four. More treated patients achieved at least one fewer support day per week at that time.

sections.title: Secondary outcomes require nuance
sections.body: In the colon-in-continuity group at week forty-eight, differences in days off support and enteral autonomy were not statistically significant. A positive primary endpoint therefore does not establish that all clinically desirable outcomes were achieved.

sections.title: What remains under evaluation
sections.body: The trial reported a generally favorable tolerability profile, but the size and duration limit detection of uncommon harms. Long-term consequences of intestinal growth and changing fluid absorption remain relevant to the benefit-risk assessment of GLP-2-directed treatment.

sections.title: Why a positive study is not approval
sections.body: Ironwood’s regulatory update states that FDA requested an additional confirmatory phase 3 study. Its 2026 update describes STARS-2. Apraglutide remains investigational, and the existence of an approved GLP-2 analog does not confer approval on this separate molecule.

profiles.name: Aviptadil
profiles.summary: Aviptadil is synthetic vasoactive intestinal peptide, a signaling molecule with vascular and immune effects. Major trials did not establish benefit for severe COVID-19 respiratory failure. A combination with phentolamine is licensed for erectile dysfunction in some countries, a different formulation and indication from investigational lung treatment.
profiles.description: VIP occurs naturally in the nervous system, gut, lungs, and other tissues. Its vasodilatory and immunologic actions prompted study of aviptadil in acute respiratory disease, including COVID-19. Early hypotheses and small reports attracted attention, but larger controlled outcomes must guide interpretation. The TESICO trial did not show a significant clinical benefit from intravenous aviptadil in severe COVID-associated respiratory failure. Separately, Invicorp combines aviptadil with phentolamine for erectile dysfunction in certain European markets. This demonstrates why a molecule cannot be assigned one global approval status without specifying the product, route, combination partner, jurisdiction, and intended condition.
profiles.mechanism: VIP signaling through VPAC-family receptors increases intracellular cyclic AMP and can relax smooth muscle and modify inflammatory-cell responses. These effects supplied a rationale for protecting alveolar tissue and altering pulmonary inflammation. Vascular relaxation also creates potential for hypotension. In erectile-dysfunction treatment, the combination with an alpha-adrenergic blocker acts locally on penile blood flow; that established product context does not validate systemic treatment of lung inflammation.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Aviptadil’s clinical meaning depends on formulation and indication. The negative respiratory trial should remain visible, while the licensed erectile-dysfunction combination must be described separately from unapproved US pulmonary or immune-health claims.

sections.title: What TESICO found
sections.body: The randomized TESICO study compared intravenous aviptadil with placebo in patients with COVID-19-associated acute hypoxemic respiratory failure. It found no significant improvement in the primary clinical outcome through day 90 and no demonstrated mortality benefit. Mechanistic plausibility and favorable subgroup narratives should not replace this overall controlled result.

sections.title: The erectile-dysfunction product is separate
sections.body: Invicorp contains aviptadil plus phentolamine and is used locally for erectile dysfunction in specified European settings. Regulatory product information describes this combination and its indication. That authorization is not an approval of aviptadil alone for ARDS, COVID-19, long COVID, or general immune enhancement in the United States.

sections.title: Route and setting change the safety assessment
sections.body: Systemic VIP activity can affect blood pressure and gastrointestinal function; aviptadil trials required close monitoring in critically ill patients. Local erectile-dysfunction therapy has a different adverse-effect context, including prolonged erection risk for the combination. Safety observations should not be moved between these routes without explaining the exposure and population differences.

sections.title: Does anti-inflammatory biology mean it treats lung injury?
sections.body: No. Laboratory mechanisms identify a hypothesis, while clinical trials determine whether the intervention improves patient outcomes. VIP’s broad biological activity makes it scientifically interesting, but the respiratory trial illustrates that target-related effects can occur without a clinically useful net benefit.

profiles.name: Bacitracin
profiles.summary: Bacitracin is an established antibiotic used in topical and certain ophthalmic products. Its former injectable products were withdrawn in the United States for safety reasons. The route distinction is essential: topical availability does not mean systemic injection remains an approved treatment.
profiles.description: Bacitracin comprises related antibiotic peptides produced by bacteria, rather than one cosmetic signaling peptide. It is familiar from first-aid ointments and prescription ophthalmic combinations. These formulations have different sterility requirements, ingredients, and intended uses. A skin ointment must not be treated as an eye preparation or injectable product. Bacitracin also illustrates why an antibiotic is not automatically the best ingredient for every healing wound. In uncomplicated post-procedure care, comparative trials can show similar overall outcomes with a non-antibiotic ointment, while allergy remains a consideration. Treatment decisions depend on the actual infection risk and clinical context.
profiles.mechanism: Bacitracin interferes with bacterial cell-wall production by disrupting recycling of a lipid carrier needed to transport cell-wall precursors. Its antimicrobial activity is directed mainly toward susceptible Gram-positive organisms. This is a direct antibacterial mechanism, not evidence of a general regenerative effect on human skin. Different organisms and infection sites require their own assessment rather than assuming universal antibiotic coverage.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Bacitracin’s usefulness is formulation- and indication-specific. Preserve the distinction between topical or ophthalmic products and withdrawn injection approvals, and do not infer that adding an antibiotic necessarily improves routine wound healing.

atAGlance.label: Not a cosmetic claim
atAGlance.value: Treating infection differs from skin rejuvenation

sections.title: What a wound-care comparison found
sections.body: A randomized trial enrolled 922 dermatologic-surgery patients with 1,249 wounds. Overall infection rates and healing outcomes did not differ significantly between white petrolatum and bacitracin, although organism-specific findings differed. Contact allergy occurred in the bacitracin arm. The study supports a context-specific interpretation; it does not mean antibiotics are unnecessary for every infected wound.

sections.title: The injectable withdrawal is a material distinction
sections.body: FDA requested voluntary withdrawal of bacitracin-for-injection applications in 2020 because of risks including kidney toxicity and anaphylaxis. A 2022 Federal Register determination states that all injection applications had been withdrawn and that withdrawal was for safety or effectiveness reasons. This history must not be hidden behind a broad approved-antibiotic badge.

sections.title: Different formulations have different rules
sections.body: Prescription ophthalmic combinations containing bacitracin remain distinct products with their own labeling. Allergy, use at the correct site, and selection for susceptible organisms remain relevant. Established topical and ophthalmic uses do not restore authorization for systemic injection. Some topical products also follow a different regulatory pathway from an individually approved new drug.

profiles.name: Balixafortide
profiles.summary: Balixafortide is an investigational CXCR4 antagonist studied in cancer and stem-cell mobilization. Early combination results in breast cancer prompted the phase 3 FORTRESS trial, which did not show the hoped-for benefit. It remains a research agent rather than an approved anticancer treatment.
profiles.description: CXCR4 helps regulate cell trafficking and interactions between cells and their surrounding tissues. Balixafortide was developed to interfere with that signaling, with interest in both hematopoietic-cell mobilization and tumor biology. A small early study combined it with eribulin in HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer and reported activity that justified further testing. The subsequent randomized FORTRESS program is essential context: adding the peptide did not improve the prespecified response outcome, and the pivotal study was terminated. These findings show why early uncontrolled combination activity cannot establish the contribution of the experimental drug. Other proposed research combinations require their own prospective evidence.
profiles.mechanism: Balixafortide antagonizes CXCR4, interfering with signaling by the chemokine CXCL12. This can alter retention, movement, and microenvironment interactions of hematopoietic, immune, and tumor cells. In oncology, the hypothesis is that disrupting these interactions may improve the effect of other treatments. The same target’s role in stem-cell mobilization does not mean that every CXCR4 antagonist has an interchangeable clinical indication.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Balixafortide has credible mechanistic and early clinical research, but the failed phase 3 breast-cancer program must remain prominent. It has no approved US anticancer indication, and related-drug approvals cannot substitute for its own outcome data.

atAGlance.label: Main completed oncology program
atAGlance.value: Eribulin combination in metastatic breast cancer

sections.title: Why early activity was not definitive
sections.body: The phase 1 eribulin combination study was single arm and involved 56 women with selected HER2-negative metastatic disease. It assessed tolerability and signs of activity, but without a randomized eribulin-only comparator it could not isolate the peptide’s benefit. Combination responses therefore supported further testing rather than an established treatment claim.

sections.title: What FORTRESS changed
sections.body: The sponsor reported that balixafortide plus eribulin did not improve objective response rate over eribulin alone in the prespecified later-line analysis. The pivotal registry lists the trial as terminated. A directory describing only phase 1 promise or merely saying phase 3 would omit the most consequential later evidence.

sections.title: Combination safety needs careful attribution
sections.body: Fatigue, neutropenia, infusion-related reactions, nausea, and other events occurred in the early combination trial. Some may relate to eribulin, balixafortide, the cancer, or their interaction. The absence of a clear early dose-limiting pattern does not establish long-term safety for other populations, standalone use, or research-vendor products.

sections.title: Does another CXCR4 drug’s approval validate balixafortide?
sections.body: No. Motixafortide has an approved stem-cell mobilization indication, but that is a different molecule, product, clinical program, and outcome. Shared receptor biology may justify hypotheses; it does not confer approval or proven anticancer benefit on balixafortide. New programs must be assessed independently of the failed breast-cancer combination.

profiles.name: Bivalirudin
profiles.summary: Bivalirudin is an established intravenous anticoagulant used during percutaneous coronary intervention, including in patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. It directly inhibits thrombin. Bleeding is the central risk, and prevention of acute stent thrombosis remains important when choosing the surrounding antithrombotic strategy.
profiles.description: Bivalirudin was designed from the thrombin-binding properties of hirudin, a natural anticoagulant originally identified in leeches. The resulting synthetic peptide acts directly without requiring antithrombin as a cofactor. Its short action and procedural evidence make it useful in selected coronary interventions, including situations where heparin is unsuitable. It is not a general-purpose chronic oral blood thinner and does not dissolve an established clot in the way a thrombolytic drug can. Clinical comparisons depend on the heparin regimen, platelet inhibitors, vascular access, and continuation strategy used, so historical trial advantages cannot be assumed to apply identically to every modern procedure.
profiles.mechanism: Bivalirudin binds thrombin at its catalytic site and an anion-binding region, inhibiting fibrin formation and thrombin-mediated platelet activation. It can act on circulating and clot-bound thrombin. Thrombin gradually cleaves the peptide, contributing to reversibility of the effect. Renal function influences clearance, so the duration and intensity of anticoagulation can change in kidney impairment even though the drug is commonly described as short acting.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Bivalirudin is a proven procedural anticoagulant with a useful role when heparin is unsuitable. Its selection balances bleeding and thrombotic risks, and results must be interpreted within the full PCI antithrombotic regimen.

sections.title: Where the approved evidence applies
sections.body: Current US labeling covers anticoagulation during percutaneous coronary intervention, including patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia or associated thrombosis. The procedural setting permits close assessment of anticoagulant effect and bleeding. This indication does not establish bivalirudin as routine long-term prevention for every clotting disorder.

sections.title: A comparison that depends on its comparator
sections.body: In HORIZONS-AMI, bivalirudin reduced major bleeding and net adverse clinical events compared with heparin plus routine glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibition in patients undergoing primary PCI. The comparator included additional platelet inhibition, which matters when applying the finding. Acute stent-thrombosis risk also requires attention rather than focusing only on bleeding.

sections.title: Bleeding and acute stent thrombosis
sections.body: Bleeding can occur at any site and may be life threatening. The label specifically warns about acute stent thrombosis in patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction undergoing PCI. Kidney impairment changes exposure, and other anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents alter the overall bleeding–thrombosis balance.

sections.title: Is it equivalent to a clot-dissolving medicine?
sections.body: No. Inhibiting thrombin limits new fibrin formation and propagation of thrombosis. Thrombolytics act on a different process to break down fibrin. Bivalirudin’s role during coronary intervention is therefore determined by the procedure and accompanying medications, not by a general claim that peptide anticoagulants remove existing clots.

profiles.name: BPC-157
profiles.summary: BPC-157 is a synthetic fifteen-amino-acid peptide studied mainly in laboratory and animal models of injury and gastrointestinal inflammation. Human evidence is limited and methodologically weak, and FDA review has not established a clinical safety or effectiveness profile for the promoted uses.
profiles.description: BPC-157 is also called bepecin or PL-14736. It attracts interest for tendon, muscle and gastrointestinal recovery, but the volume of animal publications should not be mistaken for a large body of reliable human trials. FDA’s 2026 evaluation identified small human reports, a limited ulcerative-colitis meeting abstract and substantial gaps in route-specific safety. A registered healthy-volunteer study does not supply a usable efficacy result merely because it appears in a trial registry. Claims that the molecule universally heals tissues go well beyond the available controlled human evidence.
profiles.mechanism: Preclinical studies report effects on cell migration, stress survival and tissue-repair signaling. In rat tendon-cell experiments, BPC-157 altered FAK–paxillin signaling and fibroblast outgrowth; these are mechanistic findings in experimental tissue, not a validated human receptor-based treatment model. Different injury systems and routes can produce different exposures, so an observed laboratory pathway does not establish a safe or effective clinical regimen.
profiles.keyTakeaway: BPC-157 has research interest but insufficient high-quality human evidence for routine healing claims. Evolving compounding discussions are separate from FDA drug approval and do not supply the missing clinical evidence.

sections.title: What laboratory research supports
sections.body: A tendon study found improved fibroblast migration, outgrowth and survival under experimental stress, alongside activation of FAK and paxillin. These results identify hypotheses for further investigation; they do not demonstrate faster return to sport or durable tendon healing in patients.

sections.title: What the human record can establish
sections.body: FDA’s 2026 assessment found that the small ulcerative-colitis evidence was insufficient for an effectiveness conclusion and that human safety information could not adequately characterize the proposed products. Small uncontrolled reports cannot separate treatment effects from natural recovery or concurrent care.

sections.title: Known gaps and plausible product risks
sections.body: The absence of a well-defined adverse-event rate is a gap, not reassurance. FDA highlighted uncertainty about immune reactions, peptide-related impurities and characterization. Sterility, composition and exposure also differ between proposed oral, local and injectable products.

sections.title: Compounding review is not approval
sections.body: BPC-157 was considered in the 2026 Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee process. Such review concerns compounding policy and does not establish approval of a drug as safe and effective. This record therefore avoids treating an advisory development as an approved therapeutic indication.

sections.title: Is BPC-157 the same as TB-500?
sections.body: No. They are different substances with different sequences and evidence. A combination marketed under a recovery nickname does not establish the benefit or safety of either component, and findings for one cannot be assigned to the other.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.body:
Do animal tendon findings prove faster recovery in people? No. Tendon-cell and animal experiments establish research hypotheses; they do not measure reliable clinical healing, return to sport or long-term human safety.

Does a compounding advisory discussion approve BPC-157? No. FDA's review of bulk substances and any advisory recommendation are separate from approval of a finished medicine for a specific indication.

profiles.name: Bremelanotide
profiles.summary: Bremelanotide is a prescription melanocortin agonist approved in the United States for a defined form of low sexual desire in premenopausal women. PT-141 is its development name. Evidence supports that specific indication, with meaningful cardiovascular and tolerability limitations.
profiles.description: Bremelanotide and PT-141 are two names for the same active molecule, rather than two different treatments. The approved product, Vyleesi, addresses acquired, generalized hypoactive sexual desire disorder when symptoms cause distress and are not explained by another medical condition, a relationship problem, or a medicine. This is a carefully defined clinical population. The relevant research measured changes in desire and associated distress; it did not establish a general sexual-performance enhancer. A research vial carrying the PT-141 name cannot be assumed equivalent to an approved, quality-controlled prescription product.
profiles.mechanism: Bremelanotide activates melanocortin receptors. Its clinical effect on desire is thought to involve central pathways, although the exact pathway responsible for benefit is not fully established. This differs from simply increasing genital blood flow. Receptor activity also helps explain why pigment changes and cardiovascular effects deserve attention: a peptide can influence several tissues even when the intended treatment target is specific.
profiles.keyTakeaway: PT-141 and bremelanotide have the same molecular identity and share the same clinical evidence. The approved indication is narrow, and evidence of improved desire does not establish broad performance benefits across sexes or life stages.

atAGlance.label: Approved context
atAGlance.value: Acquired, generalized HSDD in premenopausal women

atAGlance.label: Key boundary
atAGlance.value: Prescription indication does not extend to general enhancement

sections.title: What the trials established
sections.body: The RECONNECT program randomized 1,267 women across two trials lasting 24 weeks. Desire scores and distress related to low desire improved more with bremelanotide than placebo. These were questionnaire outcomes in selected participants; statistical improvement does not mean every participant experienced a clinically useful change. Most participants were White and recruited in the United States, which limits certainty about generalizability.

sections.title: Safety and suitability
sections.body: The label contraindicates use in uncontrolled hypertension or known cardiovascular disease. Transient blood-pressure increases, nausea, headache, flushing, vomiting, and sometimes persistent focal hyperpigmentation are important considerations. Slower gastric emptying can alter absorption of oral medicines. These issues make medication and cardiovascular review part of assessing suitability, rather than an optional detail.

sections.title: Approval and identity
sections.body: FDA approval attaches to the prescription product and labeled population. It does not validate every product sold as PT-141, and it does not establish efficacy in men, postmenopausal women, or people seeking enhancement without HSDD. The PT-141 name therefore does not describe an additional medicine with broader approved uses or a separate safety profile.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions
sections.body:
Is PT-141 a different peptide from bremelanotide?
No. PT-141 is a development name for the same molecule. A product sold under that name is not necessarily the approved Vyleesi formulation.

Is it approved for men or general performance enhancement?
The U.S. indication cited here is acquired, generalized HSDD in premenopausal women. Results in that population cannot establish broader enhancement claims.

profiles.name: Brilacidin
profiles.summary: Brilacidin is an investigational small molecule designed to mimic host-defense peptides, rather than a peptide itself. It has been studied in infections, oral mucositis and localized ulcerative colitis, with laboratory antiviral findings that should not be confused with proven clinical treatment benefit.
profiles.description: Brilacidin’s inclusion in peptide catalogs reflects its design inspiration, not its chemical identity. The compound was engineered to reproduce selected properties of defensins and other host-defense molecules while using a nonpeptide scaffold. Its clinical studies have used different delivery approaches, including intravenous administration, oral rinse and local intestinal administration. Each route and condition creates a separate evidence question. Activity against a virus in a cell culture does not validate an intravenous treatment for viral disease, and a small local colitis study does not establish a general treatment for inflammatory bowel disease.
profiles.mechanism: Experimental work describes interactions with microbial membranes and host-cell attachment pathways. In coronavirus cell models, brilacidin disrupted viral integrity and affected entry, including interactions involving cell-surface heparan sulfate proteoglycans. Anti-inflammatory effects are also part of its development rationale. These mechanisms depend on experimental concentration, exposure and model; their presence alone does not prove that a safe human regimen reaches the required target effect.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Brilacidin belongs in the catalog as a defensin mimetic with clinical research history, while being clearly labeled nonpeptide and investigational. Evidence must be evaluated separately for each condition and route.

sections.title: Human development programs
sections.body: The sponsor describes clinical studies in acute bacterial skin infections, oral mucositis and ulcerative proctitis or proctosigmoiditis. These differ in disease severity, exposure and outcome measures, so one program cannot establish another indication.

sections.title: What antiviral experiments show
sections.body: Studies in lung and other cell lines found inhibition of SARS-CoV-2 and several human coronaviruses. Those experiments support mechanistic research. They do not measure hospitalization, recovery, mortality or clinically achievable benefit in a patient.

sections.title: Clinical findings require their own assessment
sections.body: The COVID-19 program proceeded to a randomized phase 2 study. A sponsor update discussed disappointing topline findings and further analysis. Laboratory potency should not be used to override a clinical trial’s actual primary endpoint or to claim an approved antiviral indication.

sections.title: Route-specific uncertainty
sections.body: Safety observed with a local rinse or enema does not establish safety after systemic administration. The investigational record does not provide a generally approved dosing, interaction or long-term safety framework for unsupervised use across the proposed diseases.

sections.title: Designations are not approval
sections.body: Fast Track or Qualified Infectious Disease Product designations can support development, but do not authorize routine marketing as an effective medicine. Brilacidin remains a development compound in the primary sources reviewed.

profiles.name: Cagrilintide
profiles.summary: Cagrilintide is an investigational amylin analog developed for weight management, both alone and with semaglutide. Human trials support appetite-related weight reduction, but the single agent and the CagriSema combination have different evidence and cannot be treated as interchangeable products.
profiles.description: Amylin is a pancreatic hormone involved in meal-related satiety. Cagrilintide extends that signaling approach through a long-acting engineered peptide. A phase 2 monotherapy study established dose-related weight reduction in adults without diabetes, and later combination trials studied cagrilintide alongside semaglutide. Those programs ask different questions: one tests amylin-based treatment by itself, the other combines amylin and GLP-1 activity. A favorable combination result cannot simply be assigned to cagrilintide alone. The current knowledge base therefore retains separate canonical records for cagrilintide and the two-drug combination.
profiles.mechanism: Cagrilintide engages amylin-related receptor signaling, including receptor complexes formed from calcitonin receptors and receptor-activity-modifying proteins. These pathways influence satiation and food intake through brain circuits distinct from, but overlapping functionally with, GLP-1 signaling. Its prolonged activity supports investigation as a weekly injection. The intended mechanism is pharmacologic appetite regulation; it is not replacement for a diagnosed general amylin-deficiency syndrome.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Cagrilintide has credible human weight-management evidence, yet remains investigational. Standalone results, combination results and an eventual product label must remain distinct when assessing benefit and safety.

sections.title: What is being developed
sections.body: Monotherapy trials examine weight management in eligible adults. Combination development adds semaglutide to target another appetite pathway. These are pharmacologically related strategies but do not have identical exposure, trial populations or tolerability.

sections.title: Monotherapy evidence
sections.body: The phase 2 trial enrolled 706 adults and followed treatment for twenty-six weeks. Cagrilintide produced greater mean weight reduction than placebo, with gastrointestinal and administration-site events commonly reported. The study supported further development rather than establishing long-term cardiovascular benefit.

sections.title: What combination studies add
sections.body: REDEFINE 1 included separate cagrilintide, semaglutide, combination and placebo groups. That design helps distinguish each component from the combination. The larger average combination effect should not be advertised as the expected result from cagrilintide alone.

sections.title: What is known and still unknown
sections.body: Nausea, constipation, diarrhea and injection-site reactions appeared in monotherapy research. Longer and larger studies are needed to clarify uncommon harms, durability and use in populations not represented in early trials. A positive short-term tolerability assessment is not proof of unrestricted safety.

sections.title: Current status and product identity
sections.body: Cagrilintide remains investigational in the sources reviewed. FDA has specifically cautioned about unapproved weight-loss products containing it. Trial registration and a commercial research listing do not establish marketing approval or confirm the contents of a purchased product.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.body:
Is cagrilintide a GLP-1 medicine? It is an amylin-pathway agonist; semaglutide supplies the GLP-1 component in CagriSema.

Can CagriSema results be attributed entirely to cagrilintide? No. Combination studies assess the combined regimen and its comparators. Cagrilintide monotherapy has its own evidence, and its independent effect should be taken from the appropriate study arm rather than the combination's headline result.

profiles.name: CagriSema
profiles.molecularClass: Combination of an amylin analog and a GLP-1 receptor agonist
profiles.summary: CagriSema combines cagrilintide and semaglutide in an investigational weight-management treatment. Phase 3 studies demonstrate substantial weight reduction, but combination efficacy, adverse effects and pending regulatory review are separate from the existing approvals of semaglutide products.
profiles.description: CagriSema is a combination of two active peptides, rather than a new generic name for semaglutide alone. Cagrilintide adds amylin-related appetite signaling to semaglutide’s GLP-1 effects. The REDEFINE program has studied adults with obesity or overweight, including separate populations with and without type 2 diabetes. The sponsor filed a U.S. application in December 2025 and reported continued review during 2026. As of this review date, the combination is not treated as an approved medicine. Manufacturing or mixing the components outside the studied product does not reproduce the trial evidence automatically.
profiles.mechanism: Semaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors and influences appetite, glucose-dependent insulin secretion and gastric emptying. Cagrilintide provides prolonged amylin-related receptor activity affecting satiation. Combining the pathways aims to improve weight reduction beyond either component alone, but also combines pharmacologic burdens, especially gastrointestinal effects. The net result must be demonstrated in clinical trials rather than inferred solely from having two mechanisms.
profiles.keyTakeaway: CagriSema has strong phase 3 weight-loss evidence but remained under regulatory review at the cutoff. Its results should be attributed to the combination and population studied, with uncertainty about long-term outcomes kept explicit.

sections.title: Which populations were studied
sections.body: REDEFINE 1 enrolled adults with obesity or qualifying overweight without diabetes. REDEFINE 2 addressed overweight or obesity with type 2 diabetes. Different baseline physiology and treatments mean that results from one population do not predict identical effects in the other.

sections.title: Phase 3 efficacy
sections.body: REDEFINE 1 randomized 3,417 participants. In the treatment-policy analysis, mean weight change at sixty-eight weeks was −20.4% with the combination and −3.0% with placebo. The trial also included individual-component groups, allowing direct evaluation within that study.

sections.title: Gastrointestinal burden
sections.body: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation and abdominal pain were frequent in REDEFINE 1, usually transient and mild to moderate. A mean weight-loss benefit must be considered alongside discontinuation, tolerability and the practical ability to continue therapy.

sections.title: Head-to-head evidence
sections.body: The sponsor reported that REDEFINE 4 did not meet its primary noninferiority objective against tirzepatide. This directly comparative finding matters more than ranking drugs from unrelated trials with different durations and statistical analyses.

sections.title: Semaglutide approval does not approve the combination
sections.body: The sponsor’s 2026 filing states that the combination’s U.S. application was submitted in December 2025. Existing semaglutide approvals do not extend automatically to cagrilintide or CagriSema, and a pending application is not a final marketing authorization.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.body:
Does Wegovy approval also approve CagriSema? No. Adding cagrilintide produces a different investigational combination that needs its own regulatory assessment.

Did every comparison favor CagriSema? No. Although placebo-controlled phase 3 studies demonstrated substantial weight loss, the sponsor reported that REDEFINE 4 did not meet its primary noninferiority comparison with tirzepatide. That distinction belongs alongside the positive results.

profiles.name: Calcitonin-salmon
profiles.summary: Calcitonin-salmon is a synthetic version of the salmon calcium-regulating hormone. Injectable products have roles in selected patients with Paget disease, hypercalcemic emergencies, and postmenopausal osteoporosis. Its osteoporosis use is restricted by limited fracture evidence and a possible malignancy signal with prolonged treatment.
profiles.description: The salmon sequence is used pharmacologically because it has substantial activity at human calcitonin receptors. Injectable calcitonin can lower high blood calcium quickly and inhibit excessive bone resorption in Paget disease. US osteoporosis labeling reserves treatment for people for whom alternatives are unsuitable. Nasal and injectable products have different indications and absorption, so the route must be identified when describing evidence. Calcitonin is an older peptide medicine whose current clinical role is narrower than broad bone-health marketing suggests. European regulators restricted its long-term use after reviewing cancer findings; regulatory recommendations therefore need to be stated by jurisdiction.
profiles.mechanism: Calcitonin activates receptors on osteoclasts and reduces their bone-resorbing activity. It also changes renal calcium handling, helping lower circulating calcium. These actions make it an antiresorptive calcium-regulating drug, unlike PTH analogs that can stimulate new bone formation with intermittent exposure. Receptor adaptation and antibody formation can diminish response, so an initial biochemical effect does not guarantee durable control of the underlying disease.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Calcitonin-salmon has specific medical uses, but it is not a general bone-building peptide. Route-specific indications, limited osteoporosis fracture evidence, and the malignancy safety signal are central to interpreting its place in care.

sections.title: Approved uses depend on formulation
sections.body: The injectable label covers symptomatic moderate-to-severe Paget disease when alternatives are unsuitable, early treatment of hypercalcemic emergencies with other appropriate care, and osteoporosis more than five years after menopause when alternatives are unsuitable. Lowering calcium temporarily does not treat the cancer, endocrine condition, or other disease causing hypercalcemia.

sections.title: What is established for osteoporosis?
sections.body: The current injectable label states that fracture-reduction efficacy has not been demonstrated. This qualification should remain visible even though some historical nasal-spray trials reported vertebral-fracture findings. European review concluded that the long-term osteoporosis benefit did not justify the identified cancer risk and recommended withdrawal of the nasal osteoporosis indication.

sections.title: Important safety considerations
sections.body: Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, can occur. Excessive calcium lowering may cause muscle spasms or seizures. Long-term studies of nasal and investigational oral formulations found more malignancies than placebo; the injectable label does not exclude a similar risk with prolonged systemic use. Response can also fall as antibodies develop.

sections.title: Is nasal calcitonin interchangeable with injections?
sections.body: No. Formulations differ in approved conditions, exposure, and practical use. An osteoporosis nasal product should not be represented as emergency treatment for severe hypercalcemia. For every route, the intended duration and continuing need require reassessment because the balance of benefit and risk changes with the condition being treated.

profiles.name: Carnosine
profiles.summary: Carnosine is a naturally occurring dipeptide investigated for antioxidant and anti-glycation properties. Skin research includes experiments on excised human tissue. These studies support a mechanistic rationale, but they do not establish a sunscreen effect or broad clinical reversal of skin aging.
profiles.description: Carnosine combines beta-alanine and histidine. It occurs naturally in tissues and is used as an ingredient in some cosmetic and supplement products. In the reference skin context, interest centers on oxidative stress and glycation, processes that can affect proteins and skin structure. A compound’s ability to influence those processes in an experimental system is a useful starting point, not a complete product claim. Excised human skin preserves more tissue complexity than a single-cell culture, yet it lacks the full living person’s circulation, repeated exposure patterns, and clinical outcomes. Oral supplementation and topical application also remain separate evidence questions.
profiles.mechanism: Carnosine can participate in buffering and reactions involving reactive carbonyl compounds and oxidative stress. Skin experiments investigate whether these properties reduce molecular changes induced by light exposure. The relationship between a laboratory reduction in reactive species and a visible, durable improvement in human skin is not automatic. Mechanistic antioxidant activity must also be distinguished from a measured sun-protection factor or prevention of skin cancer.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Carnosine has plausible antioxidant and anti-glycation biology, with relevant tissue-model evidence. That is not equivalent to a demonstrated sunscreen, an established anti-aging therapy, or proof that every carnosine-containing product produces meaningful clinical changes.

atAGlance.label: Key limitation
atAGlance.value: No automatic transfer to sunscreen or clinical claims

sections.title: What the human-skin model found
sections.body: A 2024 study exposed cultured human skin biopsies to simulated solar radiation and tested topical L-carnosine. It reported changes in reactive oxygen species, advanced glycation end products, and selected gene-expression markers. The preparation was tested on excised tissue, not in a randomized trial measuring sunburn, wrinkle improvement, or disease prevention in living participants.

sections.title: Why the endpoints matter
sections.body: A lower oxidative-stress marker can justify further study, but does not tell us how large a visible benefit will be, how long it lasts, or whether ordinary product use delivers comparable exposure. Multi-ingredient products also require controls that separate the peptide from moisturization and other antioxidants. These are testable gaps, rather than evidence of either guaranteed benefit or complete inactivity.

sections.title: Product and route limits
sections.body: Cosmetic status is not FDA drug approval. Findings from topical tissue experiments do not establish the safety or efficacy of injections, and oral supplement claims require their own human data. A complete product should be evaluated for tolerability and its actual claimed outcome instead of relying on the ingredient’s natural occurrence.
