profiles.name: Humanin
profiles.summary: Humanin is a mitochondrial-derived peptide investigated in cell survival, insulin action and aging biology. Animal experiments and human biomarker associations are intriguing, but there is no established human therapeutic role for injected humanin or proof that it extends human lifespan.
profiles.description: Humanin belongs to a family of short peptides associated with mitochondrial genetic sequences. Research includes native humanin and engineered analogs such as HNG, which can differ substantially in potency and exposure. Studies report protection from experimental cellular stress, altered insulin action in rodents and associations between circulating levels and age-related characteristics in people. These lines of evidence should remain separate. An association with healthy aging does not demonstrate that giving the peptide causes healthy aging, and effects of an engineered analog do not automatically define the benefit or risk of native humanin sold commercially.
profiles.mechanism: Humanin research involves several cell-survival and metabolic pathways rather than one fully validated clinical target. In an insulin-clamp study, central administration influenced peripheral insulin action through hypothalamic STAT3 signaling, while a potent analog produced related effects after peripheral administration in rodents. Such mechanistic experiments can establish pathway involvement in that model, but do not provide human exposure, delivery or long-term safety requirements.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Humanin is a research signal with promising mechanistic observations, not a validated anti-aging intervention. Native peptide, engineered analogs, animal treatment and human biomarker associations should not be collapsed into one efficacy claim.

sections.title: Insulin-action experiments
sections.body: An original study found improved insulin action with central humanin exposure and peripheral administration of potent derivatives in rodents. It implicated hypothalamic STAT3 signaling. These experiments do not establish an approved diabetes treatment or a comparable effect from routine human injection.

sections.title: What longevity research actually measured
sections.body: A later study reported lifespan effects in worms, metabolic and inflammatory effects in mice, and higher circulating levels in children of centenarians than comparison participants. Those are different experimental and observational findings, not a human lifespan-extension trial.

sections.title: Why HNG is not simply another label
sections.body: HNG is an engineered humanin analog used in some experiments. A change in sequence can alter potency, receptor interactions and exposure. A product described only as humanin should not inherit every result obtained with a modified analog.

sections.title: Unresolved human safety
sections.body: The cited studies do not establish clinical adverse-event rates, reproductive safety, interactions or consequences of prolonged human administration. Cell-survival activity itself is not a sufficient safety argument because biological effects depend on tissue, disease and exposure.

sections.title: Do higher natural levels prove supplementation works?
sections.body: No. A biomarker can reflect health, compensation or other confounding factors. Establishing a treatment requires controlled administration studies with clinically relevant outcomes, rather than assuming that reproducing an associated laboratory value will reproduce the associated health state.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.body:
Do higher humanin levels in some long-lived groups prove that supplementation extends life? No. An association can reflect other biological differences and cannot establish a treatment effect.

Is HNG identical to native humanin? No. HNG is a modified analog used in some experiments. Its results should retain that identity instead of being attributed automatically to an unmodified humanin product.

references.title: Humanin: a novel central regulator of peripheral insulin action.
The mitochondrial derived peptide humanin is a regulator of lifespan and healthspan.

profiles.name: Icatibant
profiles.summary: Icatibant is a prescription peptide for acute hereditary-angioedema attacks. It blocks bradykinin B2 receptors and has randomized clinical evidence. U.S. labeling covers adults; approval and age ranges may differ elsewhere. It is not a general treatment for allergic swelling.
profiles.description: Icatibant is a ten-amino-acid analog designed to prevent bradykinin from producing its vascular effects. In hereditary angioedema, excessive bradykinin activity can cause painful or dangerous swelling. Firazyr and generic icatibant products address acute attacks rather than correcting the inherited cause. The disease context matters because swelling can arise through different biological pathways. A medicine effective in bradykinin-mediated HAE cannot automatically be assumed effective in histamine-mediated allergy or every case of drug-associated angioedema. Its skin-category placement reflects visible swelling, while abdominal and airway manifestations are also important parts of the clinical condition.
profiles.mechanism: Icatibant competitively antagonizes the bradykinin B2 receptor. Blocking that receptor reduces bradykinin-mediated increases in vascular permeability and associated symptoms. This mechanism acts downstream from kallikrein inhibition and is distinct from replacing C1 inhibitor. Receptor selectivity explains the treatment rationale, but clinical trials and product labeling are still needed to define the populations and attacks for which benefit is established.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Icatibant is an established acute HAE medicine with a specific bradykinin mechanism. Keep the indication, local labeling, and emergency implications of airway swelling visible rather than grouping every form of swelling together.

sections.title: The FAST-3 controlled trial
sections.body: For cutaneous or abdominal attacks, FAST-3 randomized 43 participants to icatibant and 45 to placebo. Median time to at least a 50% symptom-severity reduction was approximately two hours with icatibant versus nearly twenty hours with placebo. The study supports faster relief in the investigated HAE setting; its findings should not be generalized to unrelated swelling mechanisms.

sections.title: Local reactions and clinical context
sections.body: Injection-site reactions are common. The label allows trained patients to self-administer the approved product, but that does not remove the need for an established clinical plan. Laryngeal attacks require immediate medical attention even after treatment because airway compromise can remain dangerous.

sections.title: Specific approval, separate research questions
sections.body: The U.S. label covers adults with acute HAE attacks. Pediatric authorizations and other uses must be checked by jurisdiction. Research in other bradykinin-related conditions is a distinct evidence question; biological plausibility alone does not expand the approved indication. Approval of a finished prescription product also does not validate an unregulated research preparation.

profiles.name: IGF-1 DES
profiles.molecularClass: Truncated 67-amino-acid insulin-like growth factor I analog
profiles.summary: IGF-1 DES is an experimental IGF-1 variant lacking the first three amino acids of the native hormone. It interacts less strongly with certain IGF-binding proteins, altering activity in laboratory systems. Cell and animal findings do not establish human muscle-building efficacy, a safe administration regimen, or regulatory approval.
profiles.description: Native IGF-1 has 70 amino acids and circulates in a tightly regulated system involving binding proteins. Removing its first three residues produces des(1–3)IGF-I, a research reagent used to study how those binding proteins modify growth-factor action. Greater potency in some cell assays reflects altered availability to receptors, rather than a universal multiplier of benefit in the human body. Animal studies have examined growth and protein balance in catabolic or renal-disease models. These are not controlled human performance trials. The compound is distinct from mecasermin, an approved recombinant human IGF-1 medicine with its own narrow indication and safety requirements.
profiles.mechanism: The truncated molecule can stimulate IGF receptor signaling while escaping some of the sequestration imposed by IGF-binding proteins. In experimental systems this changes effects on DNA synthesis, protein synthesis, and protein breakdown. The response depends on the binding proteins and receptors present in the model. Reduced binding-protein affinity should not be equated automatically with a predictable duration, tissue specificity, or therapeutic advantage in humans.
profiles.keyTakeaway: IGF-1 DES is a preclinical growth-factor tool, not an established muscle-recovery medicine. Its altered binding-protein interactions explain laboratory activity but do not supply human efficacy, safety, or equivalence to approved mecasermin.

atAGlance.label: Research feature
atAGlance.value: Reduced interaction with some IGF-binding proteins

sections.title: What the cell studies show
sections.body: Experiments comparing IGF molecules found that binding proteins inhibited native IGF-1 and IGF-2 more than des(1–3)IGF-I in the tested systems. This supports a mechanism for greater apparent potency where binding proteins limit exposure. It does not show preferential delivery to an injected muscle or a proven clinical anabolic effect.

sections.title: Growth findings in a disease model
sections.body: In rats with reduced renal mass, IGF-related treatments improved growth-related and nitrogen-balance measurements, with des(1–3)IGF-I affecting protein breakdown measures. The animals, illness, exposure, and endpoints differ substantially from healthy adults seeking muscle gain. Translation requires human pharmacology and controlled clinical outcomes, which these experiments do not provide.

sections.title: Why a safe human profile cannot be assumed
sections.body: IGF signaling affects metabolism and cell growth in multiple tissues. The cited experiments were not designed to determine human hypoglycemia risk, organ effects, or long-term tumor-related consequences. Those remain unresolved concerns rather than quantified risks for this analog. Research-product identity and sterility introduce further uncertainty beyond the molecule’s experimental biology.

sections.title: Is it an interchangeable version of mecasermin?
sections.body: No. The missing residues deliberately change biological interactions, and the approved human IGF-1 product has a separate sequence, clinical program, and indication. A shared receptor pathway does not create therapeutic equivalence. No conclusion about safe human use of IGF-1 DES can be drawn solely from approval of another IGF medicine.

references.title: Insulin-like growth factor (IGF)-binding proteins inhibit the biological activities of IGF-1 and IGF-2 but not des-(1-3)-IGF-1.
IGF-I and its variant, des-(1-3)IGF-I, enhance growth in rats with reduced renal mass.

profiles.name: IGF-1 LR3
profiles.molecularClass: Engineered 83-amino-acid insulin-like growth factor I analog
profiles.summary: IGF-1 LR3 is a laboratory growth-factor analog with an N-terminal extension and an arginine substitution. These modifications reduce binding to certain IGF-binding proteins and alter biological potency. Human therapeutic benefit is not established, and animal research raises concern that growth stimulation can also accelerate tumor growth.
profiles.description: Long R3 IGF-I contains the IGF-1 sequence modified at position three plus a 13-amino-acid extension, producing an 83-residue molecule. It was developed as a research reagent for studying receptor and binding-protein contributions to growth-factor action. The word long describes the extended sequence; it should not be treated as a clinically validated human half-life claim. Its use in cell culture and animal models is much better established than any human therapeutic use. Marketing for muscle gain often omits this distinction and may confuse the analog with approved native-sequence IGF-1 treatment. These are separate molecules with different evidence and regulatory histories.
profiles.mechanism: LR3 IGF-I can activate growth-factor signaling while binding less strongly to some IGF-binding proteins. That changes the fraction available to interact with receptors. Early experiments showed that its relative potency varied with the cell system, especially whether binding proteins were present. Consequently, reduced binding-protein affinity does not mean greater activity in every tissue or a universally superior biological effect.
profiles.keyTakeaway: IGF-1 LR3 is an experimental growth-factor analog with no established human treatment role. Greater activity in selected laboratory systems is context-dependent, and preclinical tumor findings argue against presenting muscle-growth effects as inherently selective or safe.

atAGlance.label: Modification
atAGlance.value: 13-residue extension and Arg at IGF-1 position 3

atAGlance.label: Safety signal
atAGlance.value: Accelerated tumor growth in a mouse cachexia model

sections.title: Potency depends on the experimental system
sections.body: The original analog study found stronger activity in certain cells that secreted IGF-binding proteins. In a cell system lacking detectable binding proteins, Long R3 IGF-I was less potent than native IGF-I. That result directly contradicts a simple claim that LR3 is always a fixed number of times stronger.

sections.title: Muscle preservation can carry a tradeoff
sections.body: In a mouse cancer-cachexia study, LR3 IGF-I limited loss of muscle mass but also accelerated tumor growth. This is an animal finding and does not quantify human cancer risk. It does demonstrate why a growth-promoting intervention cannot be assumed to act only on desirable muscle tissue.

sections.title: Human risk remains undefined
sections.body: The cited preclinical studies do not establish human pharmacokinetics, an acceptable exposure range, or long-term metabolic and proliferative safety. IGF-related hypoglycemia and tissue-growth concerns require direct investigation for this molecule. Claims of predictable local action or a standardized long duration in humans exceed the evidence reviewed here.

sections.title: Does an IGF-1 medicine’s approval cover LR3?
sections.body: No. Native-sequence recombinant IGF-1 and LR3 are different products. A research analog that changes binding-protein interactions needs its own manufacturing controls, clinical evidence, and regulatory authorization. There is no FDA-approved LR3 indication for muscle gain, rehabilitation, anti-aging, or treatment of cachexia.

profiles.name: Insulin analogs (multiple)
profiles.molecularClass: Engineered insulin peptide hormones; multiple distinct medicines
profiles.summary: Insulin analogs are a family of essential diabetes medicines engineered to provide meal-related or sustained insulin activity. They have extensive clinical evidence, but differ in action profile, concentration, delivery device and approved use; medication mix-ups or inappropriate substitution can cause dangerous glucose changes.
profiles.description: This family includes rapid-acting analogs such as lispro, aspart and glulisine, and basal analogs such as glargine and degludec; detemir is another established basal analog. Each product has its own formulation, concentration and delivery compatibility. Insulin replaces or supplements a hormone that is essential for glucose regulation, particularly in type 1 diabetes. It is not a general muscle-building or anti-aging peptide. A family-level overview can explain common biology, but treatment decisions require the exact insulin, device, monitoring information and clinical context.
profiles.mechanism: Insulin binds the insulin receptor and promotes glucose uptake in muscle and fat while suppressing hepatic glucose production. It also affects protein and lipid metabolism and shifts potassium into cells. Amino-acid changes and formulation technologies alter absorption and duration, producing meal-time or basal profiles. These pharmacokinetic differences are clinically consequential even though the medicines share the same fundamental receptor pathway.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Insulin analogs are established, potentially lifesaving medicines whose differences matter. The specific product, concentration and delivery system must remain visible; a generic peptide label is not enough to guide substitution or use.

sections.title: Basal and meal-related roles
sections.body: Basal insulin provides background action, while rapid-acting formulations address meal-related needs or other specifically prescribed roles. Pump, intravenous and subcutaneous permissions vary by product and concentration; they are not universal properties of every insulin analog.

sections.title: How benefit is evaluated
sections.body: Insulin trials assess glycemic control and hypoglycemia alongside practical treatment performance. A useful regimen balances glucose exposure against low-glucose events, rather than pursuing a single laboratory target without regard to safety and daily function.

sections.title: Acute and local adverse effects
sections.body: Hypoglycemia can be life-threatening. Potassium shifts can cause hypokalemia, and serious allergy can occur. Repeated use at the same site can produce lipodystrophy or localized amyloid deposits, altering absorption and glucose response.

sections.title: Why concentration and device must be explicit
sections.body: Different concentrations and pen systems create medication-error risks. Product labels warn against sharing pens and require particular handling when changing regimens. A nominal volume or a syringe marking is not a universal insulin-dose equivalence.

sections.title: What a family record cannot replace
sections.body: Meal patterns, physical activity, kidney or liver impairment and other medicines can change insulin requirements. This overview deliberately supplies pharmacology and safety context rather than an individualized regimen; the exact medicine and glucose data are necessary for prescribing decisions.

profiles.name: Ipamorelin
profiles.summary: Ipamorelin is an investigational ghrelin-receptor agonist that stimulates growth hormone release. It has early human pharmacology data and was studied for postoperative bowel recovery, without significant efficacy in a small randomized trial. Claims for muscle gain, fat loss, and anti-aging are not established therapeutic indications.
profiles.description: Ipamorelin was developed as a relatively selective growth hormone secretagogue within the GHRP family. Early animal work found less stimulation of some other pituitary hormones than comparator peptides, but that does not establish a universally side-effect-free human profile. Healthy-volunteer studies examined intravenous pharmacokinetics and GH release. A later trial investigated postoperative ileus because ghrelin signaling also affects gastrointestinal motility. None of these programs establishes a routine wellness indication or validates arbitrary subcutaneous combinations sold by clinics. FDA has specifically discussed the limited safety information for compounded ipamorelin and the uncertainty of extrapolating findings across routes of administration.
profiles.mechanism: Ipamorelin activates the growth hormone secretagogue receptor, also called the ghrelin receptor, in the hypothalamic–pituitary system and other tissues. This can trigger GH secretion and affect gastrointestinal motility. It acts through a different receptor from GHRH analogs such as sermorelin. Early experiments suggested relative endocrine selectivity, but receptor selectivity and clinical safety are different questions, particularly when treatment is repeated or combined with other agents.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Ipamorelin demonstrates biological activity, but meaningful benefit for bodybuilding, recovery, or aging remains unproven. The postoperative trial did not establish efficacy, and safety findings from one formulation or route cannot validate another.

atAGlance.label: Pivotal limitation
atAGlance.value: No significant efficacy in small ileus trial

sections.title: What the clinical studies support
sections.body: A healthy-volunteer study demonstrated GH release after intravenous ipamorelin. In a randomized postoperative study, the key endpoint was time to tolerance of a standardized solid meal; the difference from placebo was not statistically significant. The population and outcome also differ substantially from the muscle-building claims commonly made online.

sections.title: How should safety reports be interpreted?
sections.body: FDA notes serious adverse events, including deaths, in the intravenous gastrointestinal-motility literature and insufficient information for certain other injection routes. These events occurred in a postoperative population and do not by themselves prove drug causation. They do prevent a confident claim that ipamorelin has a settled, benign human safety profile.

sections.title: Investigational status
sections.body: Ipamorelin is not an FDA-approved medicine. FDA also raises concerns about immune reactions, aggregation, unnatural amino acids, and impurity characterization in compounded preparations. A compound’s ability to release GH is not a regulatory authorization for treating age-related symptoms, obesity, or athletic injuries.

sections.title: Does selectivity mean no cortisol or metabolic effects?
sections.body: The original selectivity findings came largely from experimental systems and animals. They cannot guarantee the endocrine response in every human or under repeated combined treatment. Demonstrating a smaller effect on one hormone does not answer questions about glucose regulation, fluid retention, product purity, or long-term outcomes.

profiles.name: Kisspeptin-10
profiles.molecularClass: Ten-amino-acid kisspeptin fragment and KISS1 receptor agonist
profiles.summary: Kisspeptin-10 is a short reproductive-signaling peptide studied in human endocrine physiology. Small experiments show that it can stimulate LH and sometimes testosterone, but this does not establish an approved treatment for infertility, low libido or testosterone deficiency.
profiles.description: Kisspeptin-10 is the active ten-amino-acid end of the kisspeptin family encoded by KISS1. It acts upstream of GnRH and is useful for studying how the brain regulates reproduction. Human research includes brief controlled exposure in healthy men and a small study in men with type 2 diabetes and mild biochemical hypogonadism. These studies examine hormone secretion rather than long-term clinical outcomes. The wider kisspeptin literature also includes kisspeptin-54 and other analogues, which must not be treated as interchangeable evidence for this exact fragment or for products sold outside clinical research.
profiles.mechanism: Kisspeptin-10 activates KISS1R, historically called GPR54, on the reproductive neuroendocrine pathway. This can stimulate GnRH secretion and subsequently pituitary LH and FSH release, with downstream effects on gonadal hormone production. Response depends on exposure pattern and the physiological state of the axis. A short-lived rise in LH demonstrates biological activity but does not by itself establish sustained improvement in fertility, symptoms or sexual function.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Kisspeptin-10 has credible human evidence of endocrine activity but no established approved therapeutic indication. Its small physiology studies, uncertain long-term safety and differences from kisspeptin-54 limit claims about fertility, libido or testosterone treatment.

sections.title: What has kisspeptin-10 shown in people?
sections.body: A controlled study in healthy men demonstrated increased LH secretion and changes in LH pulsatility during intravenous kisspeptin-10 exposure. A separate small study in men with type 2 diabetes and mild biochemical hypogonadism showed LH and testosterone responses. Neither establishes durable symptom improvement or a fertility treatment.

sections.title: Are sexual-desire trials evidence for this fragment?
sections.body: Some frequently cited sexual-processing and desire studies administered kisspeptin-54. For example, a randomized study in women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder used that longer peptide. Such results can inform the broader pathway but should not be relabeled as trials of kisspeptin-10.

sections.title: What is known about safety and product quality?
sections.body: FDA identifies potential immunogenicity, peptide-impurity and active-ingredient-characterization concerns for compounded kisspeptin-10. Available safety information for proposed administration routes is inadequate. Short research exposures cannot establish the safety of repeated use, different routes, pregnancy exposure or products with uncertain identity and purity.

sections.title: Does a rise in LH mean fertility has improved?
sections.body: No. Hormone secretion is an intermediate biological measurement. Fertility depends on many additional factors, and meaningful evidence would include outcomes such as sperm production, ovulation or live birth in appropriate populations. Kisspeptin-10 remains investigational rather than an FDA-approved fertility or libido medicine.

profiles.name: KPV
profiles.summary: KPV is a three-amino-acid fragment associated with α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone research. It has shown anti-inflammatory activity in mouse colitis and cell-delivery experiments, but these findings have not established an effective, safe treatment for human inflammatory bowel disease or skin conditions.
profiles.description: The name KPV describes the amino-acid sequence lysine, proline and valine. Research focuses on whether this small peptide can influence inflammatory signaling while avoiding some effects of the full parent hormone. Two important distinctions are the biological model and the delivery system: a mouse receiving a specially engineered nanoparticle formulation is not equivalent to a person taking a commercially sold capsule or injection. The 2026 FDA compounding review addresses the lack of an established human product profile. This catalog includes the research without presenting it as approved gut repair.
profiles.mechanism: KPV has reduced inflammatory readouts in experimental systems, including models of colitis. Some effects appear partly independent of melanocortin-1 receptor signaling, so it should not be described simply as a miniature version of every α-MSH action. Delivery to intestinal epithelial cells and macrophages is a major research issue. Nanoparticle targeting can change tissue exposure and therefore is part of the intervention, not a neutral packaging detail.
profiles.keyTakeaway: KPV’s evidence is preclinical and formulation-dependent. Mouse inflammation findings justify investigation, but do not establish human efficacy, a standard clinical route or a known long-term safety margin.

sections.title: Animal colitis findings
sections.body: An original study found improvement in inflammatory measures in two mouse colitis models. Experiments in animals with impaired MC1 receptor function suggested that at least part of the response did not require that receptor.

sections.title: Why formulation changes the evidence
sections.body: A later study loaded KPV into hyaluronic-acid-functionalized nanoparticles within a hydrogel. This improved targeted delivery and mouse colitis outcomes relative to comparison systems. It does not establish equivalent activity for unformulated oral KPV or injected products.

sections.title: What has not been demonstrated
sections.body: These studies do not establish remission, prevention of complications or improved quality of life in people with ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease. Histologic improvement in a chemically induced mouse model is a different endpoint from sustained human disease control.

sections.title: The human safety gap
sections.body: FDA’s 2026 assessment considered inadequate human exposure and safety information among the key concerns. A small peptide can still have uncertain immune, impurity and formulation-related risks; absence of documented reactions in a limited literature is not proof of safety.

sections.title: What regulatory discussion means
sections.body: KPV-related bulk substances were reviewed for possible compounding use in 2026. A compounding-policy discussion does not create an FDA-approved KPV drug or demonstrate that a particular commercial formulation treats inflammatory disease.

profiles.name: Lanreotide
profiles.summary: Lanreotide is an approved somatostatin analog for acromegaly, selected gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors and carcinoid syndrome. It suppresses hormone secretion and can delay tumor progression in a defined tumor population, while requiring attention to gallbladder, glucose and digestive effects.
profiles.description: Somatuline Depot provides sustained lanreotide exposure through a deep subcutaneous formulation. In acromegaly, the aim is control of excessive growth-hormone activity when surgery or radiotherapy is inadequate or unsuitable. In unresectable, well- or moderately differentiated gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, its role includes improving progression-free survival. It also reduces reliance on short-acting rescue treatment for carcinoid syndrome. Control of flushing or diarrhea, normalization of hormone levels and slowing tumor progression are different outcomes, and the appropriate endpoint depends on the disease being treated.
profiles.mechanism: Lanreotide mimics somatostatin, an inhibitory hormone with receptors on endocrine and neuroendocrine cells. Receptor activation suppresses growth hormone and several gastrointestinal or pancreatic secretions. In responsive tumors, receptor signaling can also reduce proliferative activity. Suppressing insulin, glucagon and digestive secretions explains why treatment can change blood glucose and cause fat malabsorption alongside its intended endocrine effects.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Lanreotide is a specialist endocrine and oncology medicine with established uses. Symptom improvement does not by itself establish tumor shrinkage, so hormone tests, imaging and treatment tolerance remain separate parts of follow-up.

sections.title: Which tumors are covered
sections.body: The tumor indication concerns adults with unresectable, well- or moderately differentiated, locally advanced or metastatic gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. It does not cover all cancers or every tumor with a neuroendocrine label.

sections.title: Tumor-control evidence
sections.body: CLARINET studied lanreotide in advanced enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors and demonstrated longer progression-free survival than placebo. The principal finding was delayed progression in the enrolled population; this should not be described as proof that every treated tumor shrinks or is cured.

sections.title: Adverse effects and precautions
sections.body: Gallstones and related complications, abdominal symptoms, injection-site reactions and glucose disturbances are recognized. Bradycardia and thyroid-function changes can occur. New greasy stools, bloating or unintended weight loss may suggest pancreatic exocrine insufficiency rather than deterioration of the original disease.

sections.title: How response is assessed
sections.body: Acromegaly follow-up considers GH and IGF-1, while tumor care also uses imaging and clinical assessment. Diabetes and heart-rate-lowering medicines can complicate management. The label recommends attention to glucose, gallbladder and relevant thyroid abnormalities.

sections.title: How it differs from a tracer
sections.body: Lanreotide delivers a pharmacologic somatostatin signal. Radiolabeled dotatate compounds instead attach an imaging or therapeutic isotope to a receptor-targeting peptide. Sharing a receptor family does not make these products interchangeable.

profiles.name: Larazotide acetate
profiles.summary: Larazotide acetate is an investigational intestinal-barrier peptide studied chiefly as an adjunct to a gluten-free diet in celiac disease. Early symptom results were mixed, and its pivotal celiac program was discontinued; it is not an approved way to make gluten exposure safe.
profiles.description: Also known as AT-1001 or INN-202, larazotide was developed to influence epithelial tight junctions, the structures that help control movement between intestinal cells. A randomized phase 2 study enrolled adults with persistent celiac symptoms despite a gluten-free diet. Only the lowest studied group met the primary symptom endpoint, while higher groups did not. The subsequent phase 3 celiac program did not deliver an approval and was discontinued in 2022. Other investigational interest does not reverse that evidence history or validate broad claims about treating an undefined 'leaky gut' syndrome.
profiles.mechanism: Larazotide is intended to regulate tight-junction behavior and reduce excessive paracellular permeability. Development research links its activity to pathways involved in gliadin-associated barrier disruption rather than directly digesting gluten or eliminating celiac autoimmunity. The mechanism is biologically plausible but does not establish that treated patients can safely abandon dietary avoidance, nor that all gastrointestinal symptoms arise from the same barrier defect.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Larazotide has human research history but no established celiac treatment role. Mixed early findings and a discontinued pivotal program should be included whenever its intestinal-barrier mechanism is discussed.

sections.title: The question studied in celiac disease
sections.body: The phase 2 trial studied persistent symptoms in adults already following a gluten-free diet for at least a year. Participants continued that diet. It was an adjunct-treatment study, not a demonstration that larazotide could replace dietary management.

sections.title: Mixed dose-group results
sections.body: Among 342 randomized adults, the lowest studied group improved the prespecified gastrointestinal symptom score compared with placebo. The two higher groups did not differ from placebo. This nonuniform result limits a simple claim of proven efficacy across exposures.

sections.title: What happened to phase 3
sections.body: A 2022 SEC filing reports the decision to discontinue further development of larazotide in celiac disease. The later-stage program therefore cannot be cited as successful confirmation of the earlier symptom findings.

sections.title: What early tolerability can establish
sections.body: Adverse-event findings in the phase 2 study were broadly comparable with placebo. That supports the tolerability assessment of that study, but does not establish long-term safety in all populations or safety of unverified products sold for unrelated indications.

sections.title: Does it permit gluten consumption?
sections.body: The evidence does not establish protection from celiac injury during unrestricted gluten exposure. Symptom improvement, intestinal permeability and mucosal disease control are distinct endpoints. A quieter digestive tract would not by itself prove that celiac inflammation is controlled.

profiles.name: Leuprolide
profiles.molecularClass: Synthetic GnRH agonist peptide; formulation-specific depot medicines
profiles.summary: Leuprolide is an established GnRH agonist used to suppress sex-hormone production. Different approved products serve advanced prostate cancer, endometriosis, selected preoperative fibroid-related anemia and central precocious puberty. Its formulations and indications must be distinguished rather than treated as interchangeable.
profiles.description: Leuprolide is a synthetic analogue of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, supplied in several injection and depot formulations. Continuous exposure initially stimulates and then suppresses pituitary signaling, reducing testosterone or ovarian estrogen. The same biological action is useful in several diseases, but treatment objectives differ: controlling androgen-dependent cancer, reducing endometriosis symptoms, improving anemia before fibroid surgery with iron, or suppressing early central puberty. Product labels differ in delivery, duration, population and permitted combinations. A label for a prostate-cancer depot therefore cannot be assumed to describe a pediatric or gynecologic preparation.
profiles.mechanism: Leuprolide activates pituitary GnRH receptors, initially increasing LH and FSH release. Sustained exposure then desensitizes the pituitary response and reduces gonadotropin secretion, lowering gonadal sex steroids. The initial stimulation can cause a temporary symptom flare before suppression occurs. Longer-term hypoestrogenism or androgen deprivation explains several adverse effects, including hot flushes, sexual symptoms, bone loss and relevant metabolic changes.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Leuprolide has multiple established indications, but each belongs to a specific product and clinical pathway. Hormonal flare, bone health, metabolic effects and treatment duration require attention; shared active ingredient does not make different depots interchangeable.

atAGlance.label: Delivery
atAGlance.value: Several distinct depot or injection products

sections.title: Which product is intended for which condition?
sections.body: US labels separately describe prostate-cancer Lupron Depot, pediatric Lupron Depot-PED and gynecologic Lupron Depot. The fibroid indication concerns preoperative hematologic improvement with iron in patients with bleeding-related anemia. Endometriosis labeling addresses symptom control and, in specified circumstances, norethindrone add-back therapy.

sections.title: How should benefits be interpreted?
sections.body: The prescribing information reports clinical studies for the relevant formulation and indication. Testosterone suppression is a key prostate-cancer endpoint; pediatric assessment includes stimulated hormone responses, pubertal progression and growth; gynecologic studies evaluate symptoms, lesions or anemia. These outcomes should not be collapsed into a general claim of hormone optimization.

sections.title: What risks differ across treatment settings?
sections.body: Tumor flare can worsen prostate-cancer symptoms early in treatment. Labels address bone loss, pregnancy-related harm, psychiatric effects, seizures and severe skin reactions. The prostate label also covers metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease and QT effects; pediatric labeling includes intracranial hypertension. Monitoring should follow the actual product and population.

sections.title: Does add-back therapy cancel the intended effect?
sections.body: In approved endometriosis regimens, norethindrone add-back is used to reduce certain consequences of estrogen suppression, including bone loss, while treating symptoms. This does not mean every leuprolide use needs the same combination. The gynecologic label specifies limits on duration and circumstances for retreatment.

profiles.name: Linaclotide
profiles.summary: Linaclotide is an oral, locally acting peptide for constipation disorders. Current U.S. labeling covers adult chronic idiopathic constipation, IBS with constipation from age seven and pediatric functional constipation from age two, with a boxed dehydration warning for younger children.
profiles.description: Linzess acts mainly within the intestinal lumen rather than requiring substantial systemic absorption. The intended outcomes are easier and more frequent bowel movements and, in IBS-C, improvement in associated abdominal symptoms. Diagnosis matters because constipation can result from obstruction, medicines, pelvic-floor problems or other diseases that a secretory agent does not correct. The October 2026 label contains broader pediatric indications than older summaries. Age thresholds differ by diagnosis, so an age-appropriate approval for functional constipation should not be mistaken for approval of every constipation-related condition in that child.
profiles.mechanism: Linaclotide and its active metabolite bind guanylate cyclase-C on intestinal epithelial cells. Increased intracellular cyclic GMP stimulates chloride and bicarbonate secretion through CFTR, drawing fluid into the lumen and accelerating transit. Extracellular cyclic GMP has reduced activity of pain-sensing nerves in animal experiments. That mechanistic observation helps explain development but should be distinguished from clinical symptom outcomes in people.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Linaclotide is a regulated treatment for specific constipation disorders, with age limits that depend on diagnosis. Local action does not eliminate risk: severe diarrhea and dehydration remain central safety concerns.

sections.title: Current approved populations
sections.body: U.S. labeling includes IBS-C in adults and children seven or older, chronic idiopathic constipation in adults, and functional constipation in children two or older. These indication-specific ages supersede older descriptions that restricted all pediatric use to age six or above.

sections.title: What trials measure
sections.body: Randomized IBS-C studies assessed both abdominal pain and complete spontaneous bowel movements. This distinction matters: more frequent stool passage and less abdominal pain are related but separate outcomes. Pediatric approvals rely on age- and indication-specific development, not simply extrapolation from adult doses.

sections.title: Diarrhea and dehydration
sections.body: Diarrhea is the major adverse effect and can be severe. Abdominal pain, gas and distension also occur. The boxed warning addresses serious dehydration in children younger than two, for whom the medicine is contraindicated.

sections.title: When the diagnosis changes the decision
sections.body: Known or suspected mechanical gastrointestinal obstruction is a contraindication. A secretory bowel medicine should not be treated as a way to push through an unexplained obstructive process. Persistent or changing symptoms can require reassessment of the original diagnosis.

sections.title: Does local action mean no systemic concerns?
sections.body: Minimal absorption limits direct systemic exposure, but excessive intestinal fluid loss can still have whole-body consequences. The relevant safety question is therefore both where the peptide acts and what the resulting diarrhea or dehydration does to the patient.

profiles.name: Liraglutide
profiles.molecularClass: Acylated human GLP-1 receptor agonist peptide
profiles.summary: Liraglutide is an approved daily GLP-1 medicine used in different products for type 2 diabetes and chronic weight management. Its cardiovascular evidence applies to defined diabetes populations, and the diabetes and weight-management products have different eligibility and prescribing requirements.
profiles.description: Victoza and Saxenda contain the same active peptide but are not identical treatment plans. Victoza is a diabetes medicine with cardiovascular-risk reduction for certain adults with type 2 diabetes; Saxenda is a weight-management product for eligible adults and adolescents. Current Saxenda labeling includes patients aged twelve and older with obesity who weigh more than sixty kilograms. A brand’s approved condition, age group and formulation determine the relevant evidence. Weight loss can occur during diabetes treatment, but that observation alone does not erase distinctions between the products or justify combining GLP-1 medicines.
profiles.mechanism: Liraglutide resembles endogenous GLP-1 and activates its receptor. This promotes glucose-dependent insulin release, reduces inappropriate glucagon secretion and affects appetite and gastric emptying. Acylation increases protein binding and, with resistance to enzymatic breakdown, extends its action beyond that of native GLP-1. The resulting pharmacokinetics support daily administration, unlike several later weekly GLP-1 analogs.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Liraglutide has established metabolic benefits when matched to the correct product and indication. Gastrointestinal tolerance, diabetes co-treatment, relevant endocrine history and long-term response guide its clinical use.

sections.title: Weight management versus diabetes care
sections.body: Saxenda labeling covers obesity and qualifying adult overweight alongside diet and physical activity. Victoza’s diabetes indication and cardiovascular indication are separate. Saxenda’s safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients with type 2 diabetes have not been established.

sections.title: Cardiovascular evidence
sections.body: LEADER enrolled adults with type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk and found fewer major cardiovascular events with liraglutide than placebo. This supports the specified diabetes indication; it is not direct evidence of the same outcome in every younger person using liraglutide solely for weight management.

sections.title: Major adverse effects and exclusions
sections.body: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and constipation are common. Label warnings include pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, dehydration-related kidney injury and severe gastrointestinal reactions. A personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2 is a contraindication because of the thyroid C-cell tumor concern.

sections.title: Clinical issues beyond body weight
sections.body: Heart rate, glucose when relevant, gastrointestinal tolerance and hydration can influence follow-up. Insulin or insulin secretagogues increase hypoglycemia concerns. Planned anesthesia, pregnancy and significant gastroparesis require attention to current product information and clinical assessment.

sections.title: Can the products be combined?
sections.body: Saxenda labeling does not recommend coadministration with other liraglutide products or another GLP-1 receptor agonist. Switching between daily and weekly agents requires a prescribing decision rather than treating their nominal amounts as equivalent.

profiles.name: Lixisenatide
profiles.summary: Lixisenatide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist used for adult type 2 diabetes, including in a fixed combination with insulin glargine. It has a prominent effect on gastric emptying, and its cardiovascular trial demonstrated safety without establishing a cardiovascular-event reduction advantage.
profiles.description: The standalone medicine was approved as Adlyxin, while Soliqua 100/33 combines lixisenatide with basal insulin glargine. These products must be distinguished because the combination adds insulin’s hypoglycemia and medication-error risks. Current DailyMed information confirms the combination’s adult type 2 diabetes indication. Lixisenatide is not an approved obesity treatment or a replacement for insulin in type 1 diabetes. Its place in diabetes care depends on the actual product, renal function, gastrointestinal tolerance and the broader regimen rather than the assumption that all GLP-1 agents have identical outcome evidence.
profiles.mechanism: Lixisenatide activates GLP-1 receptors to support glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppress inappropriate glucagon release and delay gastric emptying. The gastric effect contributes to control of post-meal glucose but can also change absorption of oral medicines. In a fixed insulin-glargine combination, the two components address different parts of glycemic control; the combination is not equivalent to lixisenatide alone.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Lixisenatide is established diabetes pharmacology with product-specific use. Its combination with insulin and its neutral cardiovascular-outcome trial should remain explicit when comparing it with other incretin medicines.

sections.title: Standalone and combination roles
sections.body: Adlyxin’s label covers adult type 2 diabetes. Soliqua is also an adult diabetes product but contains both insulin and lixisenatide. The combination is not recommended for diabetic ketoacidosis and has not been studied with prandial insulin.

sections.title: Cardiovascular trial interpretation
sections.body: ELIXA studied patients with type 2 diabetes after a recent acute coronary event. Lixisenatide was noninferior to placebo for the cardiovascular safety endpoint, but did not show superiority. This should not be rewritten as the cardiovascular benefit demonstrated by some other GLP-1 medicines.

sections.title: Adverse effects and kidney considerations
sections.body: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and other gastrointestinal symptoms are common. Pancreatitis, serious allergy, gallbladder disease and dehydration-related kidney injury are label concerns. Severe gastroparesis and end-stage renal disease require particular attention to product restrictions.

sections.title: Gastric emptying and oral medicines
sections.body: Delayed gastric emptying can alter the timing of oral-drug exposure. The label contains specific considerations for medicines whose prompt absorption matters, including some contraceptives. Anesthesia teams also need to know about GLP-1 treatment because of aspiration concerns.

sections.title: What changes when insulin is included?
sections.body: The fixed combination introduces basal-insulin activity and its associated hypoglycemia risk. Device settings, product limits and switching instructions belong to that combination’s label; they cannot be inferred from a standalone lixisenatide description.

profiles.name: LL-37
profiles.summary: LL-37 is a human host-defense peptide produced by cleavage of the hCAP18 precursor. It has antimicrobial and immune-signaling activity and has been studied topically for venous leg ulcers. A larger controlled wound trial did not show significant overall healing benefit, and systemic therapeutic use remains unestablished.
profiles.description: LL-37 forms part of innate defense at epithelial surfaces and in immune cells. Its name reflects two starting leucines and a 37-residue sequence. Biological studies show actions extending beyond direct microbial membrane effects, including recruitment of immune cells and effects on wound-related signaling. These activities motivated development of topical ropocamptide for hard-to-heal venous ulcers. The clinical record is mixed: an early small study was encouraging, whereas the later phase IIb trial did not establish benefit across the full treated population. Evidence from local wound application does not validate injected LL-37 for chronic infections, inflammatory disorders, or nonspecific immune support.
profiles.mechanism: LL-37 is generated from hCAP18 by proteolytic processing and interacts with microbial membranes and host signaling systems. Primary experiments showed recruitment of leukocytes through formyl peptide receptor-related signaling. Such pleiotropic activity can contribute to defense and repair but can also intensify inflammation in the wrong setting. Antimicrobial activity in a laboratory assay does not define a safe systemic concentration or clinical effectiveness against an infection.
profiles.keyTakeaway: LL-37 is biologically important and has human topical research, but it is not an established injectable immune therapy. The negative overall phase IIb wound result, route differences, and unresolved safety questions should guide interpretation of broader claims.

sections.title: What the venous-ulcer trial found
sections.body: The HEAL LL-37 phase IIb trial studied topical LL-37 with compression care in 148 treated participants. The overall population did not show significantly improved healing compared with placebo. A post hoc large-ulcer subgroup suggested possible benefit, but that finding requires a prospectively designed confirmatory study rather than being presented as established efficacy.

sections.title: Human defense biology is not a dosing study
sections.body: Experiments identified LL-37 as a cleavage product of hCAP18 and showed its ability to attract human immune cells. These findings explain why researchers study it, but endogenous regulated release differs from administering a manufactured peptide. Local concentration, tissue context, and inflammatory state may change the direction and magnitude of its effects.

sections.title: Systemic safety remains unresolved
sections.body: FDA highlights possible immune reactions and impurity-characterization problems in compounded LL-37, along with insufficient human safety information for proposed uses. It also notes concerning nonclinical findings involving reproduction and tumor-related behavior in some tissues. These findings should not be converted into a precise human risk estimate, but they rule out casual reassurance.

sections.title: Can topical results justify injections for infection?
sections.body: No. The clinical trial used application to venous ulcers alongside compression, not systemic treatment of an infection. Different routes create different exposure and safety questions. Neither a favorable cell-culture antimicrobial result nor the peptide’s natural presence establishes an approved or proven injected treatment.

references.title: HEAL LL-37 randomized phase IIb venous-ulcer trial

profiles.name: LTX-315
profiles.summary: LTX-315 is an investigational cancer-treatment peptide delivered into tumors in clinical research. Early studies show local tissue and immune effects, but those observations do not establish improved survival or a broadly effective cancer therapy. Significant hypersensitivity reactions have occurred.
profiles.description: LTX-315 was developed as an oncolytic peptide: a molecule intended to damage tumor cells and potentially promote an antitumor immune response. Clinical research has involved direct injection into accessible tumors, a specialized oncology setting. It should not be confused with a cosmetic skin peptide merely because some tumors are visible in the skin or because basal-cell-carcinoma programs have been discussed. Early development separates safety, biological activity, local lesion changes, and whole-patient tumor response. These are related but different endpoints. An immune-cell increase in a biopsy is not equivalent to a demonstrated survival advantage or control of cancer throughout the body.
profiles.mechanism: The proposed action involves disruption of tumor-cell membranes and intracellular structures, releasing cellular contents that may stimulate immune responses. A phase 1 study observed tumor necrosis and increased CD8-positive T-cell infiltration in sampled lesions. These findings support biological activity in the studied setting. They do not prove that the resulting immune response is sufficient to eliminate cancer or produce durable systemic benefit.
profiles.keyTakeaway: LTX-315 remains an oncology research agent. Local tumor shrinkage and immune changes are promising experimental observations, but response criteria, serious reactions, and the absence of confirmatory outcome evidence must remain explicit.

atAGlance.label: Evidence boundary
atAGlance.value: Biological activity is not proven survival benefit

sections.title: Read the phase 1 outcomes precisely
sections.body: In a 39-patient dose-ranging study, some injected tumors shrank and biopsies frequently showed increased CD8-positive T cells. However, no partial responses were recorded under the study’s immune-related whole-patient response criteria. Reporting only local shrinkage would therefore exaggerate what the trial established. Safety and tolerability were its primary objectives.

sections.title: Later basal-cell-carcinoma research
sections.body: Verrica develops the same molecule as VP-315, also called ruxotemitide. Its later open-label basal-cell-carcinoma program reported complete histologic clearance in 51% of treated lesions, with additional exploratory response analyses. These sponsor-reported lesion endpoints differ from the early phase 1 whole-patient criteria. They do not establish equivalence to surgery, durable recurrence prevention, or regulatory approval; a 2026 update still described preparations for further development.

sections.title: Substantial reactions occurred
sections.body: Common treatment-related findings included transient hypotension, flushing, and injection-site reactions. Four participants had grade 3 hypersensitivity or anaphylaxis. These findings make the monitored oncology context essential and contradict any suggestion that a short peptide is intrinsically mild or suitable for self-directed use.

sections.title: Trial permission is not marketing approval
sections.body: A sponsor announcement concerning an accepted investigational-new-drug application describes permission to conduct research, not FDA confirmation of efficacy or commercial approval. Future studies need to establish which tumors, combinations, and patient groups may benefit, along with durability and clinically meaningful outcomes.

profiles.name: Lutetium Lu-177 dotatate
profiles.summary: Lutetium Lu-177 dotatate is an approved peptide receptor radionuclide therapy for selected somatostatin receptor-positive neuroendocrine tumors. It delivers therapeutic radiation through receptor targeting and requires specialist oncology, nuclear-medicine and radiation-safety care, including blood, kidney and liver monitoring.
profiles.description: Lutathera treats gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors in adults and children aged twelve and older when the tumors express somatostatin receptors. Patient selection depends on tumor biology, disease distribution, prior treatment and organ reserve. This is a radiopharmaceutical cancer treatment rather than a conventional hormone injection. Receptor imaging helps establish whether the target is present, while laboratory monitoring evaluates whether the patient can safely tolerate treatment. Its benefits concern tumor control in defined populations; the presence of a peptide component does not make it a general regenerative or longevity therapy.
profiles.mechanism: The dotatate component binds somatostatin receptors, with greatest affinity for SSTR2, and is internalized by receptor-expressing cells. Lutetium-177 emits beta radiation that damages the targeted cell and nearby cells. The same targeting principle can be paired with a diagnostic isotope, but therapeutic radiation produces different exposure and toxicity. Normal receptor-expressing tissues and renal handling also contribute to treatment considerations.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Lu-177 dotatate is established targeted radiotherapy for eligible neuroendocrine tumors. Demonstrating receptor expression is only one part of selection; organ function, marrow reserve and radiation precautions remain essential.

sections.title: Approved disease scope
sections.body: The U.S. indication includes somatostatin receptor-positive gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors of the foregut, midgut and hindgut. Eligibility is not established by a tumor name alone; receptor expression and clinical assessment guide selection.

sections.title: Pivotal treatment evidence
sections.body: NETTER-1 compared Lu-177 dotatate plus long-acting octreotide with high-dose octreotide in progressive midgut neuroendocrine tumors. It showed substantially improved progression-free survival. The controlled evidence supports tumor control and should not be presented as universal cure or guaranteed symptom relief.

sections.title: Major treatment risks
sections.body: Bone-marrow suppression, kidney toxicity and liver toxicity require monitoring. Delayed myelodysplastic syndrome and leukemia are recognized risks. Hypersensitivity and neuroendocrine hormonal crises can occur, and radiation can harm a fetus or affect fertility.

sections.title: Why treatment requires specialist infrastructure
sections.body: Amino-acid support, laboratory follow-up and radiation-protection procedures are part of the labeled treatment framework. Medical personnel and household contacts can be exposed to radiation from the patient or excreta, so institution-specific release and home-safety instructions matter.

sections.title: A positive scan is not a complete treatment decision
sections.body: Receptor-targeted imaging indicates where a radiolabeled peptide accumulates. It does not independently establish adequate marrow, kidney or liver reserve or determine the best place of radionuclide treatment among other oncology options.

profiles.name: Lutetium Lu-177 vipivotide tetraxetan
profiles.molecularClass: PSMA-targeted radioactive small-molecule ligand with a peptide-like binding motif
profiles.summary: Lutetium Lu-177 vipivotide tetraxetan, marketed as Pluvicto, delivers targeted radiation to PSMA-expressing prostate cancer. Its US indications expanded in July 2026 to include selected metastatic hormone-sensitive disease with an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor, in addition to defined resistant-disease settings.
profiles.description: Pluvicto combines a PSMA-binding ligand, a metal-binding chelator and the radioactive isotope lutetium-177. It is a radioligand cancer medicine rather than a conventional hormone peptide. Patient selection requires an appropriate PSMA-positive imaging assessment and attention to disease stage and previous therapy. The current US label covers metastatic androgen pathway modulation-naïve or sensitive disease with an ARPI, and specified resistant disease after an ARPI. The latter includes patients considered suitable to delay taxane chemotherapy or previously treated with a taxane. It is administered by teams equipped for radiopharmaceutical treatment and radiation protection.
profiles.mechanism: The ligand binds prostate-specific membrane antigen on target cells. Lutetium-177 then emits beta radiation that damages DNA in PSMA-expressing cells and nearby tissue, potentially causing cell death. PSMA expression is not exclusive to tumor tissue, so targeting does not eliminate exposure of normal organs. Renal elimination, bone-marrow effects and cumulative radiation exposure remain clinically relevant despite the treatment’s molecular targeting.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Pluvicto is an approved targeted radioligand with indication-specific randomized evidence and an expanded 2026 US label. Eligibility depends on PSMA imaging and treatment history, and progression benefits must be distinguished from demonstrated survival results in each trial population.

atAGlance.label: Latest US expansion
atAGlance.value: July 31, 2026: hormone-sensitive disease with an ARPI

atAGlance.label: Major monitoring
atAGlance.value: Blood counts, kidney function and radiation safety

sections.title: How did the indication change in 2026?
sections.body: FDA approved Pluvicto with an ARPI for adults with PSMA-positive metastatic androgen pathway modulation-naïve or sensitive prostate cancer, previously termed metastatic hormone-sensitive disease. The resistant-disease indication also remains: previous ARPI therapy plus suitability to delay taxane chemotherapy or prior taxane treatment.

sections.title: Which outcomes have been demonstrated?
sections.body: VISION established progression and overall-survival benefit in a previously treated resistant-disease population. PSMAfore supported earlier use before taxane chemotherapy through improved radiographic progression-free survival; its overall-survival comparison was not statistically significant. PSMAddition supported the 2026 hormone-sensitive indication through improved radiographic progression-free survival. These populations and endpoints are different.

sections.title: What does targeted radiation still put at risk?
sections.body: The label warns about cumulative radiation exposure, severe myelosuppression, kidney toxicity, embryo-fetal harm and male infertility. Fatigue, dry mouth and nausea are among common adverse effects. Blood counts, kidney function and radiation-protection procedures are integral to treatment rather than optional additions.

sections.title: Is a PSMA scan the treatment itself?
sections.body: No. PSMA imaging helps identify suitable disease and select patients, while Pluvicto delivers therapeutic radiation. A positive scan alone does not establish eligibility without the relevant clinical and treatment-history criteria. The radiopharmaceutical must be handled in an appropriately equipped clinical service.

profiles.name: Mazdutide
profiles.molecularClass: Dual GLP-1 and glucagon receptor agonist peptide
profiles.summary: Mazdutide is a dual GLP-1/glucagon agonist approved in China for weight management and type 2 diabetes. It has randomized clinical evidence, but Chinese authorization should not be confused with FDA approval or identical eligibility and availability in other countries.
profiles.description: Developed as IBI362 and LY3305677, mazdutide combines appetite-related incretin signaling with glucagon receptor activity. Innovent announced China’s first approval for weight management in June 2025 and a subsequent type 2 diabetes approval that year. The GLORY-1 obesity trial enrolled Chinese adults using locally relevant BMI thresholds. That population and regulatory context matter when interpreting the results internationally. This catalog records the medicine as approved in its actual jurisdiction, while preserving the distinction between an NMPA-authorized product and an unapproved import or research preparation elsewhere.
profiles.mechanism: GLP-1 receptor activation supports glucose-dependent insulin secretion, reduced food intake and other metabolic effects. Glucagon receptor activation adds effects on hepatic metabolism and energy expenditure, with the combined molecule designed to balance glucose and weight responses. The two targets distinguish mazdutide from GLP-1-only medicines and from GIP/GLP-1 agonists. Target count alone does not establish comparative effectiveness or safety.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Mazdutide is an approved Chinese metabolic medicine with phase 3 evidence, not a universally approved peptide. Its jurisdiction, exact indication and studied population must accompany any benefit claim.

sections.title: Chinese approval scope
sections.body: Innovent’s official announcements document NMPA approval for chronic weight management in June 2025 and for type 2 diabetes later in 2025. These authorizations concern regulated products and locally defined eligibility.

sections.title: GLORY-1 trial
sections.body: The phase 3 study randomized 610 Chinese adults with obesity or qualifying overweight. At forty-eight weeks, the higher trial group had a mean weight change of −14.01%, compared with +0.30% with placebo. The study also assessed cardiometabolic measures.

sections.title: What the trial reported
sections.body: Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most frequent and were mostly mild or moderate. Low discontinuation rates in this particular trial do not eliminate uncommon risks or show that tolerability will match in every clinical population.

sections.title: Population and endpoint boundaries
sections.body: The trial’s BMI thresholds, baseline characteristics and background care differ from many North American or European obesity trials. Indirect percentage comparisons do not establish superiority. Weight and risk-factor changes also do not substitute for a completed cardiovascular-outcomes study.

sections.title: Why approval location matters
sections.body: A medicine can be approved in China while remaining unapproved by the FDA. The applicable product information, manufacturing source and prescribing rules follow the jurisdiction, and foreign approval does not validate an online seller’s version of the ingredient.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.body:
Is mazdutide approved everywhere? No. The cited approvals are in China; they do not authorize marketing in the United States.

Does the Chinese obesity trial establish the same response in every population? No. GLORY-1 provides direct evidence in its enrolled Chinese population, while generalization to other groups, clinical settings and long-term outcomes requires additional evidence.

profiles.name: Mecasermin
profiles.molecularClass: Recombinant human insulin-like growth factor-1 protein
profiles.summary: Mecasermin is an approved IGF-1 replacement medicine for specific severe pediatric growth disorders. It is not interchangeable with growth hormone and is not an approved bodybuilding or anti-aging therapy; hypoglycemia, tissue overgrowth and malignancy-related precautions are central to its use.
profiles.description: Increlex treats growth failure in children aged two and older with severe primary IGF-1 deficiency, or growth-hormone gene deletion with neutralizing antibodies to GH. Primary IGF-1 deficiency means the problem is not simply inadequate GH secretion. The label excludes common secondary causes such as malnutrition, hypothyroidism or conventional GH deficiency. Diagnosis therefore determines whether replacing IGF-1 is biologically appropriate. Open growth plates and absence of prohibited malignancy history also matter. A low IGF-1 laboratory value alone does not establish this indication or justify use to improve strength in adults.
profiles.mechanism: IGF-1 mediates many growth-promoting effects normally stimulated by GH. Mecasermin directly activates the IGF-1 receptor, supporting cell growth and uptake of glucose, amino acids and fatty acids. Direct administration bypasses the need for GH to generate adequate IGF-1, which can be useful in selected GH-resistant conditions. Its insulin-like metabolic actions also explain the possibility of severe hypoglycemia.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Mecasermin is a targeted pediatric replacement therapy for defined IGF-1 disorders. Its indication cannot be inferred from short stature or a single low test result, and its growth and glucose effects require specialist monitoring.

sections.title: Who qualifies
sections.body: The label covers severe primary IGF-1 deficiency or GH gene deletion with neutralizing GH antibodies. It specifically states that mecasermin is not a substitute for GH in approved GH indications and is not for secondary IGF-1 deficiency from malnutrition or hypothyroidism.

sections.title: What treatment studies assess
sections.body: Long-term clinical work evaluated growth in children with severe IGF-1 deficiency. Height velocity and attained growth are the relevant outcomes. This evidence does not establish improved athletic performance, adult muscle gain or lifespan extension.

sections.title: Glucose and tissue-growth risks
sections.body: Severe hypoglycemia can occur. Other important concerns include intracranial hypertension, enlarged tonsils or adenoids, slipped capital femoral epiphysis and progression of scoliosis. Serious allergic reactions are possible.

sections.title: Growth plates and malignancy
sections.body: Mecasermin is contraindicated for growth promotion after epiphyseal closure and in pediatric patients with malignant neoplasia or a history of malignancy. The label calls for discontinuation if evidence of malignant disease develops.

sections.title: IGF-1 and GH are different treatments
sections.body: GH acts upstream to stimulate IGF-1 production; mecasermin supplies IGF-1 directly. The correct treatment depends on where the growth pathway is impaired, so one hormone cannot be substituted for the other based solely on a desire to raise a laboratory value.

profiles.name: Mechano growth factor
profiles.molecularClass: Ambiguous IGF-1 splice-variant terminology; often a synthetic E-domain peptide
profiles.summary: Mechano growth factor refers to an IGF-1 splice-variant concept and, in many products, a synthetic E-domain fragment. Laboratory studies of that fragment have conflicting results. Exercise-related gene expression is not evidence that injecting MGF or PEG-MGF improves human muscle repair, strength, or recovery.
profiles.description: The MGF label can describe different things: an IGF-1 transcript or precursor associated with mechanical loading, a short synthetic E-domain peptide, or a chemically modified product such as PEG-MGF. These are not interchangeable. Human muscle-biopsy research found changes in IGF-1 splice-variant messenger RNA after resistance exercise, which helps describe normal biology. It did not administer an MGF product. Some cell experiments reported effects of the 24-residue E-peptide on muscle progenitors, while another research group could not reproduce key effects. No approved medicine or established human recovery indication follows from this mixed preclinical literature.
profiles.mechanism: Alternative splicing changes the E-domain portion of IGF-1 precursor molecules while leaving the mature IGF-1 sequence conceptually distinct. Proposed independent actions of the synthetic MGF E-peptide include altered progenitor-cell proliferation and differentiation, but these effects remain disputed. Full-length IGF precursors and mature IGF-1 can behave differently from an isolated E-domain fragment. PEGylation creates another modified intervention whose exposure and safety require separate evidence.
profiles.keyTakeaway: MGF requires precise molecular naming and recognition of conflicting preclinical findings. A post-exercise gene-expression change does not validate injected E-peptide or PEG-MGF, and human efficacy and safety for recovery remain unestablished.

atAGlance.label: Terminology
atAGlance.value: Splice variant, precursor, and fragment are different

sections.title: What the human exercise study measured
sections.body: A small study compared IGF-1 splice-variant messenger RNA in muscle biopsies after resistance exercise in younger and older men. It found an age-related difference in the MGF transcript response. This is observational molecular evidence after exercise, not a trial showing that externally administered MGF restores youthful muscle function.

sections.title: Conflicting laboratory findings
sections.body: One study reported increased activation and fusion-related effects in cultured human muscle progenitor cells. Another group tested MGF peptides in human and mouse myoblasts and primary stem cells and did not reproduce the claimed proliferation or differentiation effects. Both results matter; omitting the unsuccessful replication overstates confidence in the proposed mechanism.

sections.title: PEG-MGF has additional unanswered questions
sections.body: FDA specifically describes a lack of human exposure data and concerns about immune reactions and peptide characterization for PEG-MGF. That modified preparation should not be treated as equivalent to endogenous IGF gene expression. The available record does not establish a safe human recovery regimen or quantify long-term metabolic and tissue-growth risks.

sections.title: Is MGF simply another name for IGF-1?
sections.body: No. Mature IGF-1, an IGF-1 precursor carrying an E-domain, the isolated MGF E-peptide, and PEG-MGF differ chemically and experimentally. An outcome from one cannot be transferred to the others without evidence. This distinction is essential when evaluating claimed studies, product labels, or proposed clinical benefits.

profiles.name: Melanotan II
profiles.summary: Melanotan II is an unapproved tanning research peptide with effects beyond skin pigment. Very small early human studies reported nausea, fatigue, and sexual effects. Case reports and regulator warnings raise additional concerns, while long-term safety and product quality remain unresolved.
profiles.description: Melanotan II is distinct from afamelanotide, historically called Melanotan I, and from bremelanotide, the approved medicine derived from a related development pathway. Similar names do not make the compounds interchangeable. Interest in tanning comes from melanocortin signaling, but that receptor family also influences other physiological functions. Commercial nasal sprays and injection products have circulated outside an established approved tanning indication. Early experiments can demonstrate that pigmentation changes occur without proving that cosmetic use has a favorable benefit-risk balance. Uncertain composition and exposure in marketed products add a separate problem from uncertainty about the molecule itself.
profiles.mechanism: Melanotan II activates melanocortin receptors involved in pigmentation and other central or peripheral responses. This broader receptor activity helps explain why tanning is not its only observed effect. The first small human pilot reported pigmentation along with nausea, somnolence, fatigue, and spontaneous erections. Mechanistic similarity to a natural hormone does not establish safe long-term stimulation or protection against ultraviolet-related disease.
profiles.keyTakeaway: Melanotan II is not the approved afamelanotide implant and is not a validated safe tanning shortcut. A tiny pigmentation study cannot establish long-term safety, and case reports should be treated as signals rather than proof of causation.

sections.title: The early human evidence is extremely small
sections.body: The initial phase 1 pilot involved only three men. It documented pharmacologic effects, including pigmentation and prolonged spontaneous erections, alongside nausea and fatigue-related symptoms. A sample this small cannot estimate uncommon harms or establish a favorable long-term profile for widespread cosmetic use.

sections.title: Pigmented lesions and uncertainty
sections.body: A published melanoma case occurred after Melanotan II use together with sunbed exposure. A case report cannot prove which exposure caused the cancer, particularly with a known ultraviolet confounder. It nevertheless reinforces why changing moles and long-term skin outcomes require serious attention rather than assuming that induced pigment is protective.

sections.title: Warnings concern both the molecule and the products
sections.body: Australia’s TGA warns against tanning products containing melanotan, including nasal and injectable forms. Such products have not passed the same assessment as an approved medicine for that purpose. Product identity, purity, and actual exposure remain additional uncertainties; changing the route does not supply missing efficacy or safety evidence.
